Removing her hands, Kara gripped the collar of her coat and sat on her for a moment longer as relief cut through her, before the sickening, skin-crawling pain of green kryptonite made her turn her attention to the knife Lena held. Plucking it from her grasp and hissing in pain, Kara tossed it aside.

 

            Pushing herself to her feet again as she ran a hand across her face, she turned slowly to look at Lex, who was watching with open interest. He looked a little disturbed that his plan wasn’t going quite as expected, his control over Lena diminished with the distance and time spent apart. He didn’t look too bothered by it though, snapping his fingers at Lena without even glancing at her.

 

            “Snowbird. Look at her; remember who your enemy is.”

 

            Brimming with rage, Kara walked over to him, staggering through the cloud of green smoke, and grabbed him by the throat, still strong enough to lift him off his feet and walk him over to the wall, where she pinned him as his feet kicked a foot off the ground and his face reddened.

 

            “I’m going to pull you apart, limb from limb,” she snarled, her voice a hoarse rasp as the kryptonite gas scorched her throat, uncharacteristically violent as she let herself become suffused with the cold hatred for this man who had taken everything from her, ruined her life. 

 

            He let out a choked laugh, fumbling in his pocket, “no, you won’t.”

 

            “You shouldn’t underestimate me.”

 

            Pushing him harder against the wall, crushing his windpipe, Kara faltered as she heard a choked, breathless sound behind her. Glancing back over her shoulder, she did a double-take at the sight of Lena collapsing to her knees, her face ashen in the red light as she clutched at her chest.

 

            Releasing Lex, who unceremoniously crumpled into a pile at the base of the wall, the small remote he held skittering across the marble as he lost his grip on it, Kara rushed over to Lena’s side and grabbed her by the shoulders, a tremor in her voice as she spoke. “What- tell me where-”

 

            Shaking her head as her face rippled with pain, Lena inhaled sharply, rubbing at her chest, right over her heart, where the pacemaker had been fitted. The shock had seized her for a moment, making it hard to breathe but it was already receding, just as her mind was narrowing to Kara’s face. To a stranger’s face. Her body stiffening, her mind going blank again as she reacted to the sight of Lex crumpled at the base of the wall.

 

            Shoving Kara out of the way, Lena’s shoes squeaked and slipped on the floor as she staggered over to his body, finding the gun at his waistband. Turning with the gun raised, pointed right at the blonde woman cautiously holding her hands up defensively, Lena stood in front of her brother’s body as he collected himself.

 

            “Shoot her,” Lex snarled.

            Lena let out a soft grumble, her brow pinching with annoyance.             “Call Alex,” she told him, watching him hesitate before running off, away from the struggle.

 

            The knot in her chest loosened with him out of the way and she shifted back off Lena’s legs, running a hand through her blonde hair and then over her face. Her lungs burned and there was a tremor in her hands as she gave Lena a tender look of weariness.

 

            “It’s alright. Just put it down.”

Bile rose at the back of her throat and she hunched over coughing and retching.

 

            “Alex, get her out,” Kara’s voice, fraught with panic, sounded distantly on Lena’s ringing ears. 

 

            She felt strong hands try to drag her to her feet and started struggling, shouting incoherently as she sobbed, clawing at the hands that grabbed her, splashing water everywhere, already equally soaked in blood and water and heedless to it all.

 

 

            “Giving her the house is generous,” Andrea commented, sitting beside Lena on the couch in the penthouse. 

 

            Tilting her glass of scotch this way and that, Lena’s mouth twisted with bitter dismay. The divorce papers on the coffee table were waiting for her signature, delivered from her lawyer that afternoon for her to read over. She hadn’t been stingy, didn’t harbour any hatred towards Kara, still loved her so much that it devastated Lena to do it but knew it was the only way out of this mess. It would never get better, so long as there were people that needed saving, fuelling Kara’s ego as she fended off attacks, heedless to how it felt to watch your wife come home beaten to a pulp, night after night, wondering when the day would come where she wouldn’t come home at all. There had been a few close calls and Lena couldn’t bear to stick around and see it happen.

 

            “Are you sure you want to do this?” Andrea asked.

 

            Wiping at the tears running down her cheeks, Lena sniffed and shrugged. “What other choice do I have? I don’t want Kal to grow up with his parents fighting all the time. I did that. I wish my parents had just divorced.”

 

            “What are you even fighting about?”

 

            Chewing on her lip, biting back the urge to tell her friend and knowing she couldn’t betray Kara’s trust like that, not even on the brink of divorcing her. Lena would never tell a soul. 

 

            “Oh … you know, it’s just- we were so young, we didn’t- we didn’t know what we were getting ourselves into. It’s just … not the life I wanted for myself.”

 

            “Have you thought about couple’s counselling? Maybe taking a break from work to sort it out? I can give Kara as much time off as she needs.”

 

            Sighing as she closed her eyes, sagging on the sofa, Lena shook her head. “None of that is going to help.”

 

            “Did you even try and work things out?”

 

            “Yes, I fucking tried. I gave her so many chances but she just wanted to ignore it all until it was too late. So this is it. This is what we’re left with.”

 

            “For fuck’s sake, Lena.”

 

            “Whose side are you on again?” Lena drawled, arching an eyebrow.

 

            Andrea scoffed, shaking her head. “This isn’t a petty argument, you’re talking about divorce here. And not an ugly one; I know you still love her. Why are you always so fucking uncompromising?”

 

 

            Kneeling on the edge of the pool, light from the hallway spilling in through the door, voices overlapping and incoherent, Lena coughed up streams of salty water, her dark hair clinging to her wet cheeks in damp strands as she hunched over. Arms crossed over her stomach, she sobbed and rocked forward, feeling her heart break, her mind break, everything breaking. 

 

            “Lena,” Kara whispered, her voice rasping but not as faint anymore as she reached out and cupped her shoulders. “It’s okay, he’s- he’s gone. He can’t hurt you.”

 

            Hitting her hand against her forehead, Lena choked on a sob, the sound jagged and breathless, holding herself together even as she fell apart. The sobs came freely now, her whole body shaking from the effort of it, and she could feel her mind furring around the edges, too much blood loss making her light-headed and weak.

 

            “Make it stop,” she whispered, pleading. “Make it stop.”

 

            “It’s okay. It’s okay, it’s stopped. It’s over,” Kara murmured, brushing her hair out of her face as she cupped her cheeks.

 

            Kara stilled then, a confused look crumpling her face as a v formed between her eyebrows. Her body was still recharging after being depleted and it took her a moment to pick up on Lena’s weakening pulse, quick and soft like a hummingbird’s, and then panic flitted across her face so quickly that Kara felt as if she’d sobered up in an instant.

 

            “Alex,” she called out, her voice frayed, “Alex, she’s hurt. You have to- please, help her. I can’t- I can’t fly, I’m still-”

 

            “Shit,” Alex muttered, pulling off Lena’s sopping coat and tearing open the front of her shirt, so soaked with blood that it was the quickest way to find out where she was hurt. 

 

            The bullet wound was small and puckered but bleeding freely, and Lena cried out as hands pressed down firmly on her abdomen, making her vision go black. She still didn’t pass out, but another memory collided with her, almost intrusive in the way it made itself known to her, dredging up the awful things she regretted saying, reminding her of what she’d forgotten.

 

 

            “I’m not staying long. I just- I wanted to give you this in person. It’s from my lawyers.”

 

            Glancing down at the manila folder clutched tightly in Lena’s hands, the guilty edge to her expression and weariness in her agonised stare, Kara let out a hollow laugh, disbelief crossing her face. “Are you fucking kidding me?”

 

            Huffing, Lena gestured helplessly, frustration momentarily clouding her face. “What did you think would happen? I’d leave for a couple of weeks and then come back? To what? The exact same shit?”

 

            Eyes stinging with tears as she gave Lena a wounded look of betrayal, Kara opened and closed her mouth, feeling as if she’d just been kicked in the chest. “I thought- I thought you’d at least … give me a chance. Talk to me.”

 

            Running a hand over her face, Lena shook her head. “There’s nothing you can say that I haven’t already thought of in my mind. Believe me, I’ve thought over every possibility, every outcome, and none of it makes a difference. I’ve already made my mind up.”

 

            “This isn’t some … fucking experiment,” Kara exclaimed, gesturing widely as she laughed, “you can’t just play it all out in your head and expect me to just … be okay with it. What the hell happened to us making decisions together? Fighting together? The Lena I married would never have given up without a fight.”

 

            “I was a fucking kid! I was eighteen ; I didn’t know the first thing about marriage, or- or being a parent. I just- I didn’t want to lose you. We met when we were kids and everything was exciting and everything we wanted was possible. And it still is, for you, for me, but not for us. Somewhere along the way … we didn’t just grow up, we grew apart and … I just don’t like the way things are anymore. It’s not good for any of us. But I still love you-”

 

            Kara reached out and cupped Lena’s face in her hands, blue eyes begging and full of guilt and pain. “Then give me another chance. Please. Give me one more chance to change your mind.”

 

            “I-” Lena started and then cut off, sighing heavily as a yearning expression crossed her face. “I want to but … you’d only be changing because I’m giving you an ultimatum. I want you to change because you want to, not because you have no other choice.”

 

            “It is a choice - you over Supergirl. It’s a choice and I’ll make it, I just- I don’t want to lose you. Come on, baby.”

 

            Lena didn’t reply, just set her mouth into a hard line, unable to speak as her throat constricted, cut off by a painful lump. She could feel her resolve wavering, wanted to give in, to try again - more than anything - but they were young and didn’t really know anything about love or themselves. Lena hadn’t ever had the chance to truly find out what kind of person she was independent of someone else, and she felt lost, adrift in her own life. 

 

            She raised the folder and then slapped it down on the kitchen counters. “To read over when you’re ready. I was fair; you get the house, I’ll cover the costs for everything Kal needs and you’ll get alimony for yourself. You can have him on the weekend - if you’re not too busy.”

 

            Turning, Lena started walking off before she fell apart, knowing that she wasn’t strong enough to stick to it if she didn’t leave now. She only managed a few steps before Kara replied behind her.

 

            “I won’t sign it,” Kara stiffly replied, a stubborn jut to her chin. “And I won’t let you take Kal from me.”

 

            Sighing, Lena didn’t turn around, just turned her head slightly and looked at the floor, unable to meet Kara’s eyes.

 

            “Don’t make it any harder than it has to be. Please.”

 

 

            The pain was debilitating and Lena screwed her eyes shut, the only thing stopping her from arching off the wet floor was Alex’s hands pressed down on her stomach. She could hear her own loud breaths, hear the uneven drumming of her head, her ears ringing as everything else became muffled and distant. She could feel the commotion nearby, other people there, more activity, but she was too far gone to pay much attention, couldn’t focus on anything.

 

            But then she felt warm fingertips against her cheek and her eyelids fluttered open, her green eyes shockingly clear and lucid as she stared up at Kara and let out a small, choked laugh as her eyes filled with tears. Her hoarse voice was loud to her own ears as her words reverberated through her chest as she pitched towards unconsciousness, body going slack as she leaned into that familiar touch that had always meant safety.

 

            “I remember you.”

22. Chapter 22

            The room was dim and cold and Lena woke feeling woozy, her eyelids heavy and her arms strapped to the bed. And the ice-cold fear cut through the drug-induced haze as she strained against the soft cuffs, a monitor beeping wildly as she thrashed, a cold sweat prickling her skin as her eyes darted around unseeingly. She was back there, in that place, in his hands, the dark cell in the cold Arctic tundra.

 

            Her breaths were constricted as panic set in, a hitching sob escaping her, and a moment later there were hands on her, making Lena shrink away. “No,” she pitifully cried, her voice small and childish as her vision blurred with tears.

 

            But the straps were being undone, her feet freed and then her hands, as a familiar voice spoke quietly, soothing her. Blinking slowly as her mind tried to piece everything together, Lena’s body went slack as she made out the figure of her wife in the dim light of the DEO medical bay.

 

            Pale and apprehensive, Kara rounded the bed and stood beside her, blue eyes roaming over every inch of Lena’s face. They stared at each other for a moment, silent, before Lena let out a choked sob and smiled thinly, the scab on her lip stinging as it pulled.

 

            “Lena.”

 

            Her name was said tentatively, nervously , as if Kara was looking at a stranger. Closing her eyes, Lena swallowed thickly, her eyes prickling as she drew in a shuddering breath, feeling the knot in her chest loosen.

 

            “Kara.”

 

            There must have been something in the way she said her name - a little more tenderness, the clarity of knowing someone, love that only came from years of knowing someone - because Kara’s face went slack, the look of hope slipping into relief. And just as quickly, her face crumpled as her blue eyes filled with tears and she let out a broken sob, sinking to her knees beside the hospital bed and grabbing fistfuls of the scratchy blankets.

 

            Fighting back her own tears as she lay limp against the thin pillows, wiping her thumb over her eyes as she fended off the assault of memories and the wave of grief, Lena ran a hand over her face and then let it fall back to the bed, swallowing thickly and clearing her throat.

 

            “It’s okay.”

 

            “I’m sorry,” Kara whispered, her voice cracking as she leaned her forehead on the edge of the bed. “I’m sorry, I- you- I didn’t- I should have-”

 

            “Shh,” Lena murmured, left hand shifting across the sheets to stroke her blonde hair, feeling a pang of longing in her chest, that ache of missing someone.

 

            Her chin dimpled with the effort it took to hold back the next sob. She sniffed and blinked up at the ceiling, a dull ache in her stomach as the effects of the drugs waned. There was the fuzzy memory of being shot, of blood covering her, the pain of something slamming into her face, and her own screams. Covering her face with her hand, Lena closed her eyes and tried to process everything as Kara quietly cried on the floor beside her.

 

            “It’s okay,” Lena murmured again, swallowing thickly as she tried to make sense of her muddled thoughts.

 

            After a moment Lena pushed herself up, gritting her teeth at the discomfort, and swung her legs off the bed. She made to stand up but Kara raised her head and gave her a stricken look, pinning her thighs to the bed.

 

            “Don’t get up. You’re hurt. You-“

 

            Lena’s drawn face ripples with amusement as her busted lips twitched slightly into a ghost of an uneven smile. Kara wiped her face on the sleeve of the DEO issued uniform and pushed herself to her feet. Her hands pushed against Lena’s shoulders and she guided her back down onto the bed.

 

            “Don’t move,” Kara whispered. “Just … stay right there.”

 

            She could read the fear in Kara’s eyes, the reserved wariness as if she didn’t dare believe this was Lena. The real Lena - although, Lena was starting to believe there was no such thing anymore. She wasn’t less of one person than the other now, just had more thoughts crammed into her mind, all of them so overwhelming that she didn’t dare dive into that pit in the centre of herself yet. 

 

            But she could feel it on the edges of her mind, the nagging reminder of things she didn’t want to acknowledge but could already feel in the dread that suffused her body, the prickling fear of things she couldn’t put her finger on yet, the overlapping timelines of things, skipping years from one moment to the next.

 

            She rubbed at her temples and breathed slowly, stifling the panic that threatened to overwhelm her. It would at some point, but she was clinging to the muffling cotton wool feeling of the drugs clouding her mind, hoping to keep out the worst of it while she focused on the now.

 

            “Are you … okay?” Lena hesitantly asked.

 

            Kara rubbed at her ribs and gave her a wan smile, pale and hollow-eyed as she rested on the edge of the bed, unable to take her eyes off Lena. “I’m fine.”

 

            Nodding, Lena chewed on the inside of her lip as she was left with her own thoughts for a moment - a terrifying prospect. Clearing her throat, she looked at Kara with a grave look on her face.

 

            “He’s dead?”

 

            Kara didn’t look at her as she nodded, fiddling with her fingers as she shook. There was a tense set to her shoulders and a muscle jumped in her jaw with the effort it was taking to keep her composure. It was hard to reconcile the Kara she’d fallen in love with with this harder, lonelier version of her, one who’d lost that childish spark in her blue eyes and didn’t smile as often. She wasn’t the Kara that Lena had fallen in love with - the first time. 

 

            Neither of them spoke and Lena’s mind flickered through dozens of memories, her face spasming with the ghost of pain, remembered snatches of conversation, her brother shouting and flickers of a car, a dog, a house on a clunky TV screen. She struggled to draw in a deep breath as she twisted her fingers in the thin bed sheets, feeling overwhelmed by her existence.

 

            “Kara?” Lena murmured, her voice trembling and thin as her eyes brimmed with fresh tears. “I don’t think I’m very well. My head-”

 

            Taking her hand as tears ran down her cheeks, Kara held it for a moment, smoothing her thumb over Lena’s fingers and knuckles, before she pressed a kiss to the back of it and then cradled it gently. “It’s alright. We’ll get you some help.”

 

            Making a vague sound of agreement at the back of her throat, Lena wiped at her cheeks and sniffed, the dull ache in her stomach growing as she became more aware of herself. Her mind sharpened too, and with it came the abundance of pain and horror that had been suppressed for so long, as well as the parts of her that hadn’t existed for years. It was all too much to bear at once, leaving her confused about what was real or not. How was she supposed to reconcile multiple personalities and what she’d done in those times with the person she’d been her entire life.

 

            They were both silent as they wiped away tears and tried to stifle the hitching sobs, and Lena couldn’t stop staring at Kara, even if she couldn’t speak, couldn’t voice her inner turmoil as violent thoughts stopped her from being able to process a thing. She wasn’t sure how long passed as Kara perched on the edge of her bed and held her hand, cheeks blotchy and breaths slowly evening out before the door opened to admit Alex.

 

            Her sister-in-law was hesitant but unwavering as she stared at Lena, her brown eyes searching and wary as she walked over to the bed. She didn’t even acknowledge that Kara was there and Lena’s eyes flickered between the two of them, remembering the tail-end of the argument she’d walked in on a few weeks ago. Clearly, it hadn’t been resolved yet but Alex had come anyway, fiercely loyal to her sister, with all the force of the DEO behind her.

 

            “You’re awake. Good. How do you feel?”

 

            Struggling to clear her throat, Lena shrugged slightly, rubbing at her heavy eyes as they prickled with exhaustion. “Fine.”

 

            “Understatement of the century,” Alex snorted. Her eyes narrowed slightly and she hesitated, forehead creasing. “Is it really you?”

 

            A thin smile flickered across Lena’s face as she closed her eyes and hummed, the sound rasping and faint. “Well, I can remember the periodic table again so …”

 

            “Oh,” Alex murmured, cocking her head to the side as a tentative smile curled her lips. “Welcome back.”

 

            Nodding, Lena swallowed thickly, her eyelids fluttering as she looked up at the ceiling. Her body was heavy and she couldn’t even think about moving, so tired and drained from the mere effort of being awake, a heaviness in her chest from the crushing knowledge of everything that had been blocked out, that Lena just wanted to sleep for eternity.

 

            “How’s she looking?” Kara quietly asked.

 

            Alex gave her a cursory look, her mouth thinning slightly as she busied herself with the beeping monitors and Lena’s chart on the tablet in her hands. “Good.”

 

            Relief threaded through Lena and she exhaled softly, welcoming the chance to sink into nothingness. She wasn’t ready to confront her new reality, and even the whispered thought of having to come to terms with the things she’d done, things she’d been forced to do was enough to make her flinch, her face taut with anguish. Mistaking her agonised expression for the pain of her gunshot wound, Kara shifted closer on the bed, free hand nervously fluttering around her.

 

            “Does it hurt? Are you-”

 

            “I’m giving her painkillers now,” Alex curtly interrupted, administering the drugs to the IV bag, the wire snaking into Lena’s arm.

 

            It didn’t take long for the drugs to kick in, mercifully numbing and making her drowsy. Lena wanted to baulk at the thought of being drugged again, the dim memories of Scopolamine withdrawal making her skin crawl as the corners of her mind blurred. Panic started to settle in then, her vision dimming as she felt dizziness sweep through her, her head reeling even as she was dragged down into unconsciousness.

 

            She was in and out for a few days after that, waking in fits and bursts as a fever ran through her and she struggled to adjust. Each time she woke, it was to the terrifying struggle of being tied to the hospital bed with the soft cuffs, protecting her from the violent thrashing as nightmares left her screaming herself hoarse. Most of it was forgotten, but the feeling persisted, a dysphoric unease that left her skin crawling and dread sitting in her stomach like lead. The painkillers treating her wound were the only relief from it all, and as much as she hated the feeling of it creeping through her veins like ice, stealing her autonomy for hours at a time, it was better than the alternative. 

 

            Being awake was its own personal torment for Lena, and she found herself unable to talk, for the most part, her throat constricting around the words on her tongue. Each time, she just ended up crying, the emotional pain and damage of what she’d endured far outweighing the small gunshot wound and the bruises and cuts on her face. There were parts of her that would never be whole again, never fully heal from her ordeal, and she was tormented by the intrusive thoughts of all the traumatic things her brother had subjected her to. The only relief was that he was dead now, that he’d never hurt her again, that he hadn’t won.

 

            She stayed at the DEO for four days, in and out of consciousness and isolated from anyone except Kara and Alex, much to her relief. Lena knew she wouldn’t have been able to face anyone else, wouldn’t be able to answer Brainy’s million questions or look Kelly in the eye, as if her friend could read her every thought, and J’onn quite literally could at that, which was an even more unbearable prospect. But they sent flowers and that was enough to bring tears to Lena’s eyes.

 

            “Alex thinks you’re fine to go home now,” Kara said on the fourth evening, sitting on a chair beside the bed, looking pale and thin and so far from the lively golden girl Lena had first fallen in love with that it hurt to think about everything they’d been through. “I’ve been talking to Kelly about- about help for you. There are … places. Centres with specialised care.”

 

            “A psychiatric hospital?” Lena rasped.

 

            Kara’s expression was pained and pleading as she grimaced. “Yes. Kelly said … well, there’s going to be a lot for you to process. Proper care for- for a while might be a good idea. I know I don’t have the right anymore but-”

 

            “You choose.”

 

            Her voice was a soft murmur, dismissive and final, not wanting to talk about it or think much at all. Lena wouldn’t fight Kara on this, knew it was the best course of action and the break she needed - the thought of going back to either of her homes was overwhelming, to say the least - and she hated to admit it but she needed professional help. She would drive herself mad without it, could already feel herself spiralling down into a pit of self-hatred, and knew she needed someone else to sit with her and organise her thoughts, explain it all and work through it.

 

            Kelly recommended one an hour out of the city, a private clinic further out in the foothills where Lena could be in long-term treatment until she was well enough to go home. Dressed in the clothes Kara had brought her, a mix of her old outfits - terribly outdated - and her ragged new ones, Lena sat in the front seat of the Range Rover as Kara drove her through the winding roads, telling her about the facilities. Morning yoga, an equestrian centre, art classes and private counselling twice daily. Lena didn’t have much of an opinion on any of it, just knew it was somewhere safe, with no reminders of anything painful.

 

            They arrived at the clinic mid-morning, the late August weather making for a clear day, the sky a pale blue and the forest surrounding them rustling in the mild breeze. It was the first time Lena had properly been outside in a while and she breathed deeply, staring at the building of cream stone and honeyed wood. It was long and low, like a luxurious ranch, and she allowed Kara to carry her bag as she trailed her inside.

 

            She had no interest in the paperwork, leaving it to Kara, who fumbled through some sections, admitting her estranged wife to the clinic with a signature on the bottom of a few pages, and was taken on a tour through the place. It was sterile but made to look homely and comfortable, the kind of place where one could heal, even if certain areas of it had a hospital feel to them. There were locks on hallways, offices and nurses' stations and closed doors leading to communal spaces that made it feel like a school at times with the tables and chairs.

 

            The nurse took her outside, to the sprawling garden with shaded benches and neatly maintained flower gardens. Patients were playing tennis on a court off to the left, a few more reading or walking. It could have been a hotel with its heated indoor pool and the Michelin star chef they employed, the twin beds made up with thousand thread sheets and psychologists and psychiatrists employed for hundreds per hour. Everyone there was celebrities, socialites and sports stars, heiresses and investment bankers, or CEOs like her. 

 

            It didn’t seem like a bad place and Lena was content to isolate herself there for the foreseeable future, hoping some time and space from everything would offer some clarity. As much as she hated to admit it, her sessions with Pete had been a reprieve from the confusion of her amnesia and new life, but she’d learned to somewhat adjust, and maybe the people at the clinic would be able to offer the same to her. Although, she didn’t think they’d ever be able to absolve her of her guilt. 

 

            The tour ended at the small private room allocated to her and Lena looked around the space with bland interest. A closed door to a small bathroom, the twin bed with the thick mattress but the unmistakable look of a hospital bed, able to strap her down if her nightmares posed a threat, a set of drawers for the clothes packed for her, a wide flat-screen TV that only allowed access to approved movies and shows, and an armchair near the wide window overlooking a small portion of the garden, letting in shafts of sunlight through the slanted blinds. The window only opened a sliver at the top for fresh air and there were no curtains, no curtain rails , no lamps with glass bulbs or anything else Lena could hurt herself with. Even her bag had been subjected to a thorough search by security and a nurse to ensure she didn’t have anything harmful with her.

 

            In the end, she was left alone with Kara to say goodbye, the door to the hallway left open - no locks - and the mere thought brought a lump to her throat. It was what was best for everyone though, what Lena wanted for herself, but she was seized by a moment of panic at the thought of being separated from her again. Although she knew they’d technically been reunited for the better part of a year now, the old version of herself couldn’t help but think of that four-year gap. It unsettled her and Lena’s heart lurched in her chest as her stomach twisted, Kara’s shoulders slumping slightly as a sheepish look of understanding crossed her face.  

 

            “Are you going to be okay here?” Kara asked, fiddling with her fingers as she lingered inside the door.

 

            Nodding, although her mouth was dry and she couldn’t bring herself to speak, Lena stared down at the floor, cracking her knuckles. The silence was unbearable but she didn’t know what to say that wouldn’t be meaningless. But there was one burning question that was making her feel uneasy.

 

            “Are you allowed to visit?” Lena asked, looking up and giving Kara an anxious look.

 

            Kara gave her a small smile. “Yeah, I am. Visiting hours are every day from ten to six. It’s just family for the first month, so I can bring Kal.”

 

            “Okay.”

 

            They stared at each other for a long moment, so much left unsaid between them that Lena didn’t even know where to begin unpacking. There wasn’t enough time to say it all now, hadn’t been time before now either, and she broke off her stare, looking down at the floor as she wrestled with the disconcerting feelings inside. Lena imagined it would be a while before they’d be able to have that conversation, sort things through and hold each other accountable, and she was fine with putting it off for now. It was inevitable, but she was happy for some time to sort herself out first. That was the purpose of this whole thing - her marriage would come second to that, and perhaps it would afford her some clarity in hindsight.

 

            “You should go,” Lena finally said.

 

            Nodding, Kara swallowed thickly, a reluctant look in her eyes, as if she was worried about them being separated again too. “Okay. Yeah. They said I should- I should give it a week … let you settle in properly before I visit, so …”

 

            Pressing her lips together, Lena nodded and rocked slightly on her heels before she lurched forward with the momentum and crossed the gap between them. Wrapping Kara in a tight hug, her face furrowed with a grave look of relief as something inside her settled. Kara’s arms slowly came up to wrap around her as well, and Lena could have cried at how it felt to be held by her, those arms so strong and familiar that some small part of her felt healed by it after so many years without. She didn’t want that hug to end, wanted to stamp her anger down, her bitterness at the lies, the regret and guilt of leaving, and scrub the last five years from her mind and continue on as if nothing had happened. There was something to be said for amnesia; at least she hadn’t been hurting so much before that it physically pained her.

 

            But she loosened her grip after a moment longer, swallowing thickly as she let go of Kara, pulling back a fraction. Kara stared at her for a moment longer, wariness creeping into her face as she lingered, unable to make herself leave. Giving her an uneven smile, forcing more bravado into it than she felt, Lena gave her a reassuring nod.

 

            “Don’t worry, I won’t disappear again. I promise.”

23. Chapter 23

            The first night, Lena didn’t sleep at all, staring up at the ceiling as she tried to dismiss the memories by counting as many digits of pi as she could - which was a fair amount, with her newly restored memory - and she found herself repeating that over and over, and when she’d exhausted it as a distraction, translating songs into Latin and then Kryptonian and Ancient Greek. It passed the hours slowly, the clinic silent save for the natural creaks and groans of a building and the rustling of trees outside. 

 

            She was tired, drained from the day of settling in and meeting new people, put into an afternoon art class, where she ended up drawing the schematics for an old L-Corp design instead of drawing anything, before she enjoyed dinner in the communal dining hall. It was like a hotel dining room, with round tables spread out and a series of tables draped in cloth and laden with a variety of dishes, sides and desserts to help themselves to. The little cakes could have been right out of a patisserie in Paris, but Lena had little appetite, eating only a few mouthfuls of food for show. 

 

            Afterwards, she’d gone back to her room and remained there ever since, changing into pyjamas when the orderlies came around to check on everyone one by one, and then allowing them to turn her lights off an hour later. They’d come through twice since, cracking open the door and sweeping a flashlight over the bed to ensure she was there, and Lena closed her eyes at the sound of the door cracking open, feigning sleep.

 

            Up before dawn, she changed into clean clothes and brushed her teeth in the mirror, but couldn’t even look at the shower as she shakily washed her hands and tried to quell the nauseous feeling in her stomach. Returning to her room, she made her bed and curled up on the armchair until the nurses came around to wake everyone and greeted her with surprise when they found her up and dressed. She picked at some fruit at breakfast and had a bite of a plain croissant, sipping two cups of coffee and being deterred when she went for a third.

 

            After breakfast, she had her first therapy session and was escorted to a room by a tall man in nurse scrubs, who knocked on the door and then gestured for her to go inside with an encouraging smile on his face. Stepping into the open doorway, Lena clenched her hands as she found herself staring at a woman, who was climbing to her feet and walking over to her.

 

            “Lena, it’s nice to meet you. I’m Doctor Park,” the woman said, holding a hand out for her to shake.

 

            Wariness crept over Lena as she limply shook the doctor’s hand, hovering just inside the doorway as Doctor Park shut it behind them, the sensation of feeling trapped making Lena tense as she tracked the woman’s movements across the small room. Like everything else in the clinic, it was opulence masking medical necessity, and there was something clinically cool about the therapy room. Pale blue walls, Scandinavian wooden furniture, framed artwork and cushions curated by award-winning interior designers, yet Lena was still met with the sensation that they were at a hospital of some kind.

 

            “Please, take a seat.”

 

            Nodding, Lena sank down onto the edge of the navy blue leather sofa, her eyes catching on the oil painting of waves and the flower arrangements and books. A wide window overlooked a patch of trees and bathed the room in sunlight but Lena couldn’t bring herself to relax.

 

            “You may not know this but I’m acquainted with Kelly Olsen. Only in passing,” Doctor Park said, trying to break the tension. “I imagine that’s why she settled on this facility.”

 

            “You know her?” Lena asked, surprise crossing her face.

 

            Giving her a slight smile, Doctor Park nodded. “I do. I also spoke with your wife about the circumstances leading you here to gain some insight into how we can help you.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “Firstly, how’re you feeling?”

 

            Lena shrugged, running her palms over her thighs, her mouth dry as she nervously looked around. “I don’t know.”

 

            “I understand. This must be difficult for you to process. Would you like to start by telling me more about it?”

 

            Lips twisting resentfully, Lena wrapped her arms around herself and drew her knees up to her chest. It felt safer that way, like she was too small to be much of a target, although she knew that it had never stopped the beatings before. 

 

            “I don’t think so,” she whispered, her eyes prickling. 

 

            Fighting back the shakiness inside her that left her stomach lurching and her heart pounding, a certain clamminess to her skin, Lena’s bottom lip quivered as she looked down. Doctor Park tried to catch her eye, a kind look on her face.

 

            “That’s okay. Why don’t you tell me a little more about yourself then? So we can get to know each other better.”

 

            Nodding as she rubbed at her eyes, trying to quieten her thoughts, Lena sniffed and considered the proposition for a moment. “I don’t really know which one’s the real me anymore. There are … too many people up here,” she whispered, touching her brow.

 

            “Perhaps they’re all real.”

 

            Deliberating, Lena pressed her lips into a flat line. “I don’t want them to be.”

 

            “Why not?”

 

            “Because … I don’t think I could live with myself if that’s true,” Lena choked out, the pain in her chest so sharp that it left her breathless, chest heaving as she closed her eyes and covered her mouth with a hand.

 

            “Lena, can you take a deep breath for me?” Doctor Park murmured.

 

            As the therapist started counting slowly, Lena tried to force herself to inhale, a painful effort as she balled her hands up in her lap and sat rigidly, feeling like she couldn’t get enough air in her lungs. Breathing for a minute as she tried to parse through the panicked feeling of horror and self-hatred, Lena slowly unwound slightly, the stiffness in her shoulders lessening as she dug the heels of her hands into her eyes.

 

            “Good. That’s good, Lena.”

 

            They were silent for a minute and Lena stared at the thickly carpeted floor as she rubbed her forehead, her hands shaking. “Can you tell me what you were feeling just now?” Doctor Park gently asked.

 

            Shaking her head, Lena’s eyes filled with tears and she hastily wiped them away as she tried to blink back the rest. Doctor Park shifted and eyed her curiously, looking completely at ease as she noted Lena’s body language, the tense set to her face, her wide eyes, frightened.

 

            “How about how you’re finding it here so far? I know it’s only been one night, but first impressions are important for how we progress.”

 

            “I couldn’t sleep,” Lena whispered.

 

            “Why not?”

 

            Mouth turning down at the corners, Lena swallowed thickly. “I’m scared.”

 

            “Of what?”

 

            “My dreams. I had nightmares before but … I couldn’t remember them. But now I remember what I did …”

 

            Humming thoughtfully, Doctor Park nodded. “Do you feel responsible for that?”

 

            “Yes.”

 

            “What is it you feel responsible for?”

 

            “All of it. Before. During. I thought … when I didn’t have my memory, I thought getting it back would fix everything. Now … I just feel like I’m going mad.”

 

            Giving her a small smile of understanding, Doctor Park leaned forward. “Well, you don’t seem mad to me, Lena. You seem like you’ve gone through a very traumatic experience - a series of them - and I’m here to help you work through that. I understand it’s all very confusing for you, but if we work together-”

 

            “Confusing?” Lena choked out disbelievingly. 

 

            “How would you describe it?” Doctor Park asked.

 

            “Fucking horrifying,” Lena sobbed, unable to even feel embarrassed as her tears came too fast now, her heart feeling like it was breaking in her chest. “I feel … sick. I can’t even look at myself, I can’t- I feel repulsed to even exist in my body, I-”

 

            Angrily wiping her face on her sleeve, her eyes sharp with her pain as her pale cheeks turned blotchy, Lena gave Doctor Park a bewildered look of grief. “How am I supposed to … go home to my wife and my kid and just act like … none of this happened?”

 

            “You won’t,” Doctor Park softly said, a grim look clouding her face. “Trauma and pain will always be something you’ll carry with you, but with my help, maybe we can lessen that burden. Help you cope with what was done to you. Some things are done to us, Lena, not by us, and we can’t carry that guilt around, seeking absolution for something out of our control. It’s debilitating.”

 

            “Yeah,” Lena breathed, deflating as the anger drained her. 

 

            They fumbled through the last twenty minutes of the session, Lena feeling on the verge of breaking every other sentence, a fresh memory bombarding her with her actions, with her injuries, before they wrapped up. There would be another one that afternoon, and potentially a meeting with a psychiatrist, if it was decided she needed medicating. Then she was encouraged to go outside, basking in the mild warmth of late August as she breathed in the sweetness of flowers and listened to bees drone and birds sing. It was somewhat freeing to be outside, and Lena was content to sit and wait until they told her to go inside for mid-morning yoga.

 

            Her days followed a routine, each part of it scheduled, whether she was booked in for arts and crafts, allocated reading time in a comfortable library or given an hour to socialise with other patients - Lena was stiff and cold to them, especially a property developer there for detoxing who thought it a great moment to try and ask her where she’d been for so many years - and her first two days passed quickly, into the third before she could even process her reality.

 

            Morning meditation was up first on the third day, Lena feeling exhausted from another sleepless night and she followed the dozen other patients into the wide room with the wall of windows overlooking the east side of the facility, getting the morning sunlight. Sitting second from the left in the third row, Lena crossed her legs as instructed and made her best effort to focus on her breathing and let her mind go empty. It was easier said than done though, the act of sitting still with no distractions leading to a torrent of awful memories crowding to the front of her mind, clamouring for attention. Face spasming with unease as her stomach knotted with dread, Lena kept twitching and shifting, the soothing music playing at a low volume doing absolutely nothing to blot out the fear that nagged at her and slowly grew with each new memory she couldn’t avoid. 

 

            It got to an unbearable point where Lena shot to her feet and lurched towards the door, her breaths rasping and uneven as she staggered out into the hallway, clutching her head as she tried to stifle the panic. A nurse followed her out, making sure she was okay and trying to coax her back inside.

 

            “Come on. Come back inside and sit down. It’s tricky, but it’s good-”

 

            “No,” Lena quietly cried, hand scrabbling at the front of her shirt as her chest constricted. “No, no, I don’t want to.”

 

            “Alright, let’s take a deep breath.”

 

            Wild-eyed and struggling to breathe, Lena backed up against the hallway wall and shook her head as two nurses sandwiched her in. The man reached out to gently cup her shoulder and she violently jerked away, face ashen and eyes frantic. 

 

            “Don’t touch me.”

 

            “It’s okay, Lena. We’re just trying to help, okay?”

 

            He reached out again to touch her, gently grabbing her arm as he spoke slowly, as if soothing a wild animal, but his words were distant and intelligible to Lena as she hunched over, crying out as if in physical pain. He ducked down to her level to try and comfort her and Lena proceeded to straighten up, headbutting his chin as he staggered back, dragging her with him. She was almost screaming by that point and another nurse rushed over with a syringe full of haloperidol as she struggled against the man’s bulk, his eyes fixated on the needle as tears wet her cheeks.

 

            She was pleading, her words garbled sobs that left her gasping for air, and a moment later she was sinking down to the wooden floor, clutching her head as she curled into a ball, crying. Doctor Park was in front of her, talking quietly, dismissing the nurses and trying to contain Lena’s fear.

 

            “Take a big breath for me, Lena,” she murmured, trying to catch her eye. “It’s alright; there are no needles. Why don’t you come with me and we’ll have a cup of tea and talk?”

 

            It was another five minutes of hitching sobs and frantic breaths that she struggled to slow before she was finally able to pick herself up off the floor, taking the tissues handed to her by the therapist and wiping her face. Doctor Park walked beside her down the wide hallway, keeping up a stream of gentle conversation as she commented on the mild morning, how they were truly into autumn now and the late-blooming flowers would be kicking in, how Lena would have to go for a walk to see them and might enjoy one of the horseback rides along a flat trail through the trees to enjoy the leaves turning.

 

            Back in Lena’s room, the door shut as Lena made for the sofa and curled up in it, leaving Doctor Park to settle on the edge of the bed as she observed quietly for a few minutes. It was unbearable and made Lena’s skin crawl as she shut her eyes and dwelled in the shaky hollowness expanding in her chest. It left her feeling raw and frightened and it took a lot longer than a few minutes for it to slowly start to shrink, her body recognising its surroundings again.

 

            A nurse brought two cups of tea on a tray and Doctor Park cradled hers in her hands while Lena left hers on the small table beside the armchair. They were left alone again, and Lena stared blankly at the wall, her cheeks blotchy from crying as she tried to lock away her emotions again. After another minute of silence, the tension in Lena’s body seeming to diffuse slightly as she was given the space to breathe and contain herself, Doctor Park cleared her throat.

 

            “The nurses say you haven’t taken a shower since you arrived.”

 

            Lena’s face prickled with burning shame as she ducked her head down, picking at her bitten nails as she clenched her teeth together to stop the trembling in her jaw. Her vision blurred with a film of tears and she couldn’t speak around the lump in her throat as she slowly shook her head, expecting to be screamed at, to be kicked in the ribs, to be drugged and tied up.

 

            “Will you tell me why?”

 

            Drawing in a shuddering breath, she exhaled sharply and clamped her lips together again. Rubbing at her tired eyes, wondering how much longer she could hold off on sleeping, she sniffed and put her head in her hand.

 

            “The shower,” Lena eventually rasped.

 

            “You don’t like the shower?”

 

            Lena’s chin dimpled with the effort to fight back a sob as she nodded. Closing her eyes, she let out a shaky breath and leaned her head back against the back of the chair. Doctor Park stayed on the edge of the bed, a safe distance away from her, watching closely with a kind look on her face.

 

            “That’s okay. What don’t you like about it?”

 

            Pain rippled across her taut features and Lena shook her head. 

 

            “It’s okay if you can’t talk about it yet. Maybe we can find a different solution until you feel comfortable. How do you feel about baths?”

 

            Lena winced as memories of that dark room, the salty taste of the pool, Kara’s bleeding body and the disorienting pain of being thrust back into her own body with the gunshot wound were all too fresh. Shrugging indifferently, Lena rubbed her eyes. It hadn’t been a problem before though and she relaxed at the memory of a hot bath, of her arm in a cast and Kara telling her she was pretty. The thought made her want to cry, the bruises on her face mottled and ghastly against her pallid skin, her hands that had seen so much blood, undeserving of being called anything short of monstrous.

 

            “It’s not as bad.”

 

            “Well, we’ll move you to one of the other rooms with a bath then.”

 

            The change was made as easy as that, Lena’s clothes moved into a room a little further down, identical save for the bath instead of a shower in the comfortable ensuite. She stayed in the room, sitting on an armchair with her hands clamped over her ears, the sound of thundering water making the hairs on her arms stand on end. The nurse only filled it a quarter of the way at Doctor Park’s direction and Lena warily endured a shallow bath, trying to get it over with as soon as possible, the water barely warm and getting colder with each minute she was in there.

 

            Washing her hair was just about all she could manage, thrashing around at the end as panic made her blind with sense, her mind consumed with murky thoughts that had her scrambling out of scant inches of water as if she’d been drowning in it. Wrapped in a towel and shaking, a few suds clinging to her skin, she dried off quickly, hands shaking as she hurriedly tried to wipe off the water rolling down her skin. Just the sight of it was enough to make her stomach turn, dread making her cold.

 

            Dressing quickly, she mechanically brushed her teeth and dressed, avoiding looking in the mirror, and ran a thumb over the row of stitches on her stomach, the edge of the wound a light shade of pink where it healed slowly. A nurse dried her hair for her and Lena was given another cup of tea and parked in front of the TV to distract herself until it was time for lunch. 

 

            That night, she fell asleep despite her struggle to stop it, waking a short while later as she screamed herself hoarse and had to be pinned down by two nurses, while a third struggled to slip the soft restraints over her wrists and ankles. The prick of the needle was lost on her in the midst of her terror but when her whole body went limp as the ice-cold feeling of the drugs swept through her system, she was keenly aware that this time she hadn’t escaped it. She murmured her protests as the sedation worked to drag her under and Lena woke in the morning to the feeling that her head had been stuffed with cotton wool, her mouth dry and eyes itching with sluggish tiredness.

 

            In therapy, she was silent and somewhat resentful as Doctor Park tried to engage her in conversation. The first twenty minutes were uncomfortable and one-sided as Lena toyed with the cuffs of her shirt and frowned at the floor, unwilling to even look up.

 

            “I know this might not be something you want to talk about, but I hope you can recognise that I’d like to help you, Lena. Understanding will help me do that.”

 

            “I don’t like talking about things. I never have. I’ve always thought therapy was a sham.”

 

            Smiling slightly, Doctor Park nodded, “a lot of people have that perception. It’s a useful tool in understanding and regulating our own thoughts and emotions though. I suppose in your terms it would be like installing antivirus software on a computer; there to help the computer screen and fix problems by pointing them in the right direction to look for anything harmful.”

 

            Blinking, Lena looked at her. “Yeah, but sometimes it’s too broken and you have to replace it.”

 

            “Except, you aren’t broken, and I think this time we … okay, I’ll admit, I’m struggling to find another computer analogy.”

 

            A ghost of a smile twitched Lena’s lips as she ran her fingers over the leather of the sofa. “We need to repair the hard drive.”

 

            “Sure. That sounds right. How do you do that?”

 

            “Run a diagnostics test.”

 

            “So, if we consider therapy the diagnostics test, what information would I need to know?”

 

            Rubbing at her eyes as she started to grow restless, Lena let out a pent up breath. “It’s the nightmares.”

 

            “When did they start?”

 

            “A few months ago. Kelly said that it was probably because the part of me that was locked away was surfacing while I was unconscious. But now …”

 

            “Now …”

 

            Eyebrows drawing together in a confused look, Lena cracked her knuckles and struggled to speak. “Now I remember and I’m- I’m afraid to sleep. If I sleep … I won’t be able to stop myself from dreaming about what I did. While I was in the hospital, I was on painkillers, but here … I didn’t sleep the first two nights, but last night … I couldn’t stop it.”

 

            “Thank you for telling me. I’d like you to meet with Doctor Hamilton later on; she’s a board-certified psychiatrist who works at the facility. A lot of our work is collaborative and she might-”

 

            “I don’t want any medications.”

 

            Silent for a moment, Doctor Park leaned forward. “It’s important that you rest properly, Lena. There are medications she can give you that would put a stop to the nightmares.”

 

            Wariness flashed across Lena’s face and she absentmindedly rubbed at her arm, still a little tender from the sedation she was given in the middle of the night. Her mouth was dry and she was slow to reply as she deliberated.

 

            “If I- if I took the medication … the needles-”

 

            “We only sedate patients who are a risk to their own safety and the safety of staff,” Doctor Park quickly replied. “If your sleep was undisturbed, there wouldn’t be any need for it - or the restraints. I know it must feel like a violation to be tied down and drugged, but it’s a safety regulation employed by psychiatric facilities. If we can avoid it, we will.”

 

            Lena’s answering smile was thin and slightly mocking, a bitterness to her hoarse voice as she replied. “I don’t like needles. Not anymore.”

 

            “Then let’s work together, and with Doctor Hamilton, to find a way around that.”

            

            It was with great reluctance that she found herself sitting in the office of another woman later that afternoon, a desk separating them and honeyed wood-panelled walls giving the place a comfortable glow in the late afternoon sunlight seeping through the blinds. She’d just taken a seat, feeling scruffy and not much like herself in her sweatpants and sweatshirt, socked feet in slippers, as she looked at the polished psychiatrist in slacks and a shirt. All of her haughty beauty was diminished with her bare, pale face and the lingering trauma in the haunted look in her eyes as she waited for the woman to speak.

 

            “Your reputation precedes you, Miss Luthor,” Doctor Hamilton said with a faint smile. “I understand that you’d prefer not to be here, but thank you for meeting with me. It might be a relief for you to know that our sessions won’t be quite so introspective in a typical therapeutic sense, and not as often as your sessions with Doctor Park.”

 

            Lena nodded, watching her with brooding eyes as she resisted the urge to curl in on herself, an unreadable expression on her face. Doctor Hamilton tapped a folder on her desk as she forged ahead with the conversation.

 

            “I hear you haven’t been sleeping well.”

 

            “No.”

 

            “Do you want to tell me a little bit about that?”

 

            “I have nightmares.”

 

            “How long have they persisted?”

 

            “Months.”

 

            The questions went on from there, everything from her history of mental health problems, previous medications, other symptoms, and whether she’d previously seen a psychiatrist. Lena struggled through some of them, her hoarse voice breaking occasionally as she tried to describe her brother’s mania, his narcissism, her mother’s detachment and casual cruelty, all of it painful and clouded by her trauma. 

 

            Doctor Hamilton listened and formulated a discussed a projected treatment plan for her, informing Lena that their sessions together would mostly be dealing with medication management, and Lena took it all in with grim resignation. The thought of medications meddling with her mind was enough to make her tense and panicked, but once she was on them perhaps her anxiety would be soothed enough by the clouding effects of the drugs for her to accept it.

 

            “Doctor Park has requested that I be transparent about the medication I’d like to prescribe you. It’s rare we get a patient with multiple PhDs and such a high IQ; I think she’s hoping this will allow you to understand better and trust the process. Have you heard of Prazosin before?”

 

            “It’s used to treat high blood pressure.”

 

            “Correct. It’s also an effective treatment for PTSD. It blocks certain alpha-1 receptors in the brain which can improve sleep and reduce nightmares by allowing blood to flow more easily. A diagnosis can take weeks, months, even years , but given the trauma you’ve endured … I think what you’re exhibiting has been a months-long attempt at trying to make your PTSD known to your conscious mind, and now you’ve been drowned in all of that trauma all at once. Prazosin will be able to help give you a reprieve from that while you sleep, and, combined with therapy, allow you to consciously focus on managing your trauma instead.”

 

            “Okay.”

 

            Lena’s voice was meek and defeated and she didn’t object to it as she sat before the psychiatrist, wishing it was all over, some part of her wishing that her mind could be wiped again. In hindsight, being a nobody with a fake ID was preferable to the hellish nightmare her mind had been blocking her from.

 

            “I’d like to start you on an initial dose of 2mg tonight when you go to bed and see how you go.”

 

            She dreaded it for the rest of the day after their session ended, and when the nurse came around at lights out, she was handed a little paper pill cup and trembled as she forced it down with a sip of water. It all but knocked her out, a side effect she’d been warned of, and she was nauseous and dizzy the rest of the following day, but she slept. 

 

            Nausea and dizziness subsided after another day and she found herself grateful and relieved at the reprieve sleep now offered her. For the rest of the week, she went to bed the moment she was given her dose and didn’t wake up until the nurses roused her in the morning, trying to minimise the number of hours she’d have to be awake. 

 

            Every day was an endurance test, prompting her to talk about things she shamefully wanted to keep buried, trying to get her to cooperate and socialise, exercise and clear her mind and everything that was the antithesis to who Lena was. No amount of people crammed into one mind would ever make her change so drastically that she would no longer retain her stubborn streak.

 

            By the end of her first week, she was tired and irritable and perhaps even more confused and anxious than before. Talking about it only brought it to the forefront of her mind and Lena didn’t care about meditation or playing checkers with the other patients. She didn’t have an artistic bone in her body - she was a scientist; why couldn’t she express herself through schematics and blueprints instead of painting her dreams as they wanted.

 

            Brooding in the garden as she tried to manage her own feelings, resorting to some of her surlier techniques from her childhood - frosty silence and avoidance - Lena was surprised to look up as someone stopped in front of her and find Kara standing there. Blinking as her face went slack, her mouth opening, she rose from the bench.

 

            “Hi.”

 

            “Hi,” Kara sighed with relief, looking as if a weight had just been lifted off her shoulders at the mere sight of Lena.

 

            Lena did look somewhat better than the last time they’d seen each other - she wasn’t quite so pale and bruised from her extensive injuries, she’d been sleeping better and the confused panic had diminished slightly in her wide green eyes. Still, there was a thin, pinched look of worry on Lena’s face, her appetite still evading her, and she trembled at the sight of Kara, so overcome with emotion that she had to sink back down onto the bench before her legs gave out beneath her.

            

            “Sorry, I- I wasn’t expecting you.”

 

            “It’s been a week,” Kara told her.

 

            “Oh. Right.”

 

            “It took everything in me not to come out here and sit on the roof all night to make sure you were okay,” Kara admitted with a sheepish laugh, sinking onto the bench beside Lena. “I thought a retired superhero lurking about right after you were admitted might have been too conspicuous. Thought you might … need the space too.”

 

            Lena nodded, hunching slightly as she wrapped her arms around herself, pale and drawn and haunted. “How are you?” she murmured.

 

            “I’m okay,” Kara softly replied. “How’re you?”

 

            She looked like she wanted to cry as she stared at Lena, and Lena did start crying when she looked up and met her concerned eyes. Clapping a hand to her mouth, Lena closed her eyes and turned her head, cheeks flushing red as she swallowed a sob. Kara was swiftly off the bench and kneeling before her, gently trying to pry Lena’s hands from her face.

 

            “Hey, hey, it’s okay.”

 

            “I know. I’m fine,” Lena murmured, wiping at her cheeks as she sniffed and then exhaled sharply.

 

            Kara didn’t know what to say for a moment, cupping Lena’s cheek as she stared up at her in agony, guilt crashing through her anew as she blamed herself for not preventing this whole thing from happening. If she’d only stayed home that day instead of taking Kal out into the mountains to let her cousin have some modicum of freedom. At four years old, he knew he couldn’t risk floating or moving too fast, do algebra while in kindergarten or anything that would have singled him out as abnormal, but those moments of freedom were the least Kara could offer him. She’d just never imagined it would be at the expense of their entire life being upturned for the second time in a handful of months - this time, only worse.

 

            “Are they treating you-” Kara started before trailing off, rigid as she looked around for a nurse, for a therapist, or anyone who she could rip into.

 

            Laying a hand on Kara’s arm, Lena let out a choked laugh. “They’re nice. I just- I just don’t feel like myself.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “I know it’ll take time, but I- it’s just … confusing . I’ve just … missed you.”

 

            Quickly moving back up onto the bench, Kara hesitated before putting an arm around her, feeling Lena press into her as she blinked rapidly. Stomach swooping with nerves as she felt the weight of everything between them, Kara struggled to speak for a moment, swallowing the lump in her throat.

 

            “I can visit you every day now,” Kara whispered. “When you’re ready, I’ll bring Kal. It’s-”

 

            “You need to go to work, and he needs to go to school. You can’t-”

 

            “I’m not letting you out of my sight again. I don’t care about work, I don’t- I don’t care about anything else right now. I just … want to help you.”

 

            “Well you can’t,” Lena curtly replied, curling her hands into fists in her lap. “This isn’t something you can punch your way through.”

 

            Raking a hand through her hair, Kara blew all the air out of her lungs and cupped the back of her neck. “I don’t do that anymore,” she murmured. “You know that.”

 

            “Well, maybe you should . You’d be better off doing that than sitting here all day.”

 

            “Don’t do this,” Kara softly pleaded. “Don’t push me away.”

 

            Letting out a breathless laugh as she wiped away a stray tear, Lena gave her an uneven smile. “I already did.”

 

            A flicker of hurt crossed Kara’s face and she nodded, a bitter twist to her lips as she swallowed. Rubbing the bridge of her nose, she climbed to her feet after a moment and held out a hand. “Come on. If you’re just going to press on things that hurt, let’s go for a walk.”

 

            Allowing herself to be pulled to her feet, Lena wrapped her arms around herself while Kara pocketed her hands, and the two of them started walking along the paved path cutting through the manicured garden. 

 

            “What’s it like here?”

 

            Lena didn’t reply, clenching her teeth as she worked to swallow, a lump closing up her throat as she walked in silence.

 

            “Please just let me know you’re okay here,” Kara whispered.

 

            “What do you want me to say?” Lena listlessly replied, her face pained and resigned. “That it’s amazing and I’m having a blast? Half of the time I feel like I’m losing my mind, the other half of the time I’m wishing I had so at least I wouldn’t have to …”

 

            “It’s okay,” Kara murmured, reaching out to touch her arm.

 

            Jerking away as her face flushed with anger, Lena blinked back stinging tears and hoarsely shouted at her. “It’s not okay. Don’t stand there and tell me it’s fucking okay. You don’t know- you don’t know-“

 

            She repeatedly smacked her palm against her forehead and doubled over, eyes tightly squeezed shut as she inhaled sharply through clenched teeth. A nurse was there, gently speaking to her as the woman tried to defuse the situation, and Lena drew in a ragged breath as she straightened up, face tilting towards the sunlight as she kept her eyes closed and focused on her breathing. They were soft gasps, her whole body trembling, and she hated that she’d been reduced to an anxious mess.

 

            “Why don’t you come inside?” the nurse gently urged her, glancing around at the other patients and guests trying to enjoy the peace of the garden.

 

            Lena wiped her face on her sleeve as she stalked back towards the long, low building, and Kara followed behind with the nurse, who was suggesting a cup of tea in a private sitting room, tucked out of the way where they wouldn’t be disturbed or disturb anyone. Allowing herself to be herded towards an available space, Lena sat cross-legged on one end of the sofa, toying with the bottom of her sweater as she stared at the rug beneath the coffee table. Kara sat at the other end and a nurse brought two cups of tea for them, Kara quietly thanking her while Lena tried to stifle the hollow queasiness in her stomach.

 

            “Drink your tea,” Kara softly told her. 

 

            Scoffing, her mouth twisting derisively, Lena curled into a ball, bristling with anger and hurt and unable to stop herself from feeling that way. “I don’t want tea.”

 

            “Shall I ask for coffee?”

 

            Shooting her a sidelong look of annoyance, Lena clenched her teeth. “You should go.”

 

            “I just got here.”

 

            “I- why are you so stubborn?”

 

            Kara let out a choked laugh, cheeks dimpling as her eyebrows rose. “Me? Pot. Kettle. Black.”

 

            Rolling her eyes as her lips twitched slightly, Lena turned, leaning against the back of the sofa as she sighed, closing her eyes. “I’m really sorry, Kara.”

 

            “You haven’t done anything.”

 

            “I feel like … this is all my fault. If I’d just- if I hadn’t-”

 

            “None of this is your fault,” Kara firmly whispered, no room for objection as she reached for Lena’s hand and squeezed it tightly. “Do you hear me? Don’t you dare blame yourself for any of this.”

 

            “You killed him for me,” Lena murmured, opening her eyes to look at her, a sheen of tears blurring her vision. 

 

            She watched a ripple of pain cross Kara’s face as she shifted on the sofa, drawing her hand back and running a hand over her face, bumping her glasses, and Lena felt a pang of guilt strike even harder. Kara looked guilty too, her distress evident in the restlessness of her movements, reaching for her tea as a momentary distraction.

 

            “I did. And I’d do it again, and again, and again,” Kara confessed.

 

            Lena gave her a long, piercing look, trying to reconcile this harder version of her wife with the one that had been so soft, so gentle and sweet and happy. In her mind, Kara jumped from one person to the other, a four-year gap of this evolution into a bitter, sad person who was angry at herself and the world.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            Kara’s head sharply rose as her mouth opened and closed, stammering for a moment as she blinked in surprise. “What?”

 

            “Thank you,” Lena rasped. “I never said thank you before …”

 

            “You don’t have to thank me; I should have done it a long time ago.”

 

            “Don’t do that,” Lena curtly replied, giving her a crooked smile of sadness. “I know you, you’re my fucking wife - don’t pretend like this is nothing for you. I know how hard that was for you.”

 

            Softly sighing, Kara put her cup down and shifted across the sofa, bridging the gap between them, and took Lena’s hands in her own warm, trembling ones. Cupping them tenderly, she looked down as her mouth hardened into a flat line and swallowed audibly.  “It wasn’t hard, and maybe that’s what makes me feel so guilty. I thought about killing him every day for four years . It was easy . It was the second easiest thing I’ve ever done.”

 

            “And what’s the first?”

 

            “It doesn’t matter now. Don’t feel bad for me though, Lena. I don’t deserve your pity.”

 

            “I don’t pity you, I- it’s just … hard for me to … you see me as two different people - who I was before, and who I was when you got me back - and … that’s how I see you now, and … I get it. I didn’t before but now I do and it’s hard to- to adjust to that.”

 

            A faint smile twitched Kara’s lips as she nodded, “yeah, it is.”

 

            Withdrawing her hands, Lena ran a hand through her hair and blew the air out of her lungs before turning to pick up her tea, taking a sip and letting it trace a warm path through her chest. She felt nervous and shy and didn’t know what to say to the one person she’d always been so honest with. It stung a little, leaving a bitter taste in her mouth that another mouthful of tea couldn’t wash away.

 

            “How’d it happen?” Kara asked after a moment.

 

            “Hm?”

 

            “I’ve been thinking about it since that night but I can’t figure it out. How’d you get your memories back?”

 

            Lena froze for a moment and her eyes locked onto Kara’s ribs before she reached out to touch her fingertips to the exact spot she’d rammed the knife. A spasm of pain made her flinch, sloshing a bit of tea on her lap before she hastily set the cup down and shied away from Kara.

 

            “He programmed it that way. The moment I hurt you enough to … to kill you, it was like it just-” Lena mimed an explosion from her head, shaking her head as she avoided looking at Kara. “Whatever was blocking it just- it vanished and everything came through at once. He wanted me to know what I’d done, on every level of myself, not just- not the new me who loved you. So I’d have to live with that guilt.”

 

            Kara let out a choked laugh, rubbing at her cheek. “His arrogance was astounding.”

 

            “I almost got you,” Lena whispered, her cheeks colouring with shame at the memory.

 

            “No, you didn’t,” Kara said, a smile in her voice. “Maybe if he didn’t make you turn the red sun lamps on. I mean, I know he had to or he never would’ve stood a chance, but … come on , he should’ve known that kryptonite is a harmless mineral on Krypton. It’s the yellow sun that makes it hurt me. All you did was pretty much stab me with an ordinary knife.”

 

            “Oh, just an ordinary knife?” Lena said with a huff of laughter, wiping her eyes. “That’s known to kill people, you know.”

 

            “Not me.”

 

            “Should we talk about your arrogance?”

 

            Giving her a small smile, Kara’s eyes shuttered and she sighed softly. “You’ve already told me in great detail what you think about that.”

 

            “Yeah,” Lena whispered, barely audible. Drawing in a shuddering breath, she grimaced. “I’m still mad at you, you know.”

 

            “I know. We’ll have a lot to sort out when you get out of here.”

 

            “That might not be for a while.”

 

            Lena’s voice was small and defeated, her stomach sinking with the knowledge that she would be there for a while. She’d tried not to think about it too much, but she knew that she wouldn’t be going home tomorrow, or even next week. It was only through a concerted effort that she was even talking about it as it was, wishing she could just curl up into a ball and never speak again, never have to unpack everything and come to terms with it all. For once in her life, Lena thought there was some truth to the term ‘ignorance is bliss’ .

 

            “That’s alright,” Kara said, a strained smile on her face as her eyes filled with mournful sadness. “Take as long as you need.”

24. Chapter 24

Days passed by, starting to blur together in a haze of therapy, tea and meditation clouded by her medication and detachment from her surroundings. Each day was much the same, leaving Lena quiet unless spoken to, and even then she was prone to remain silent, prone to restless irritation and frequent bouts of crying. The initial shock of her memories flooding back in was starting to wear off, leaving her numb and horribly empty, a cold feeling of nothingness spreading throughout her as she was left with the memory of her actions and all the time in the world to try and process it.

 

Kara visited every day, as promised, which wasn’t always a good thing. Some days Lena didn’t speak a word to her, and could have been asleep if not for her open eyes which occasionally blinked. A few times, Kara showed up to hold Lena in her arms the entire time as she bawled her eyes out, everything hurting and all-consuming, until she cried herself to sleep and Kara left her tucked into her bed. It was harder for her to leave on those days.

 

One week became two, became three, until the month came to a close and late September brought a pleasant chill to the foothills and the hidden clinic. So far, Lena hadn’t processed much of what had happened to her, even with twice-daily therapy sessions. All she had to show for herself was multiple prescriptions for antidepressants and sleeping pills and a few bare sketches of the cell, the house, the vague dark figure of her brother, all of it rudimentary as she was made to sit in the sunlit room and draw. 

 

The three different people started to merge comfortably in her mind though, sorted through and neatly arranged by her subconscious. Some of it was raised in therapy - Lena’s favourite colour was green, she liked Yiruma, not the punk music she remembered listening to on a crappy radio as Tess, she liked beer now but remembered appreciating the smoothness of a good scotch in her office. Some of it was blurry and dimmed, remembered through a haze of the cocktail of drugs her brother had pumped her with, the dim memory of repetitive hand-to-hand combat moves nestling in beside the memory of assembling computers and machines in her basement workshop, of building Lego towers with Kal. Lena knew how to stretch a budget meal for four days, save the leftovers for tomorrow, sustain herself on one meal a day, and could identify the labels of wines that cost thousands and explain the uses of different cutlery at fancy events. It all amounted to her.

 

When they said she had a visitor one morning, just as October was creeping in, adding a deeper touch of reds and oranges to the trees crowding the surrounding land, Lena expected it to be Kara again. She’d been reading one of the novels Kara brought in for her, ones she thought she might like and had missed out on over the years, and she looked up from her book at the sight of someone entirely different. Lillian stood in the doorway, dressed head to toe in designer brands, looking regal and haughty as she stared at her daughter. The book slipped from Lena’s hands.

 

            “You.”

 

“Ah, so it is you then,” Lillian murmured, a faint look of amusement on her face. “I’d wondered if it was true.”

 

“What’re you doing here?” Lena hoarsely demanded.

 

Spreading her hands slightly as she glanced around, Lillian smiled. “It’s visiting hours for family. I’m family.”

 

A rasping scoff worked its way up Lena’s throat and she toyed with the cuffs of her cardigan as she swallowed thickly, her throat tight and her face mournful. “Well, we both know that’s only a technicality. What, are you here to finish me off? Get your revenge?”
