Lillian stiffened, her pale eyes sharp with a warning, before she deflated, setting her handbag down on the drawers hosting Lena’s clothes and shedding her coat before taking a seat in the matching armchair.  “I had an inkling that one of you wouldn’t walk away from that when I told him you wanted to meet.”

 

Lena made a low sound of scepticism at the back of her throat, her face stiff and her eyes hard. “And I bet you hoped it wouldn’t be me.”

 

“The opposite, actually,” Lillian shot back, cool and impassive. “I just didn’t think you had it in you.”

 

“Well, I only finished the job. But you can thank him for making me into enough of a monster to do that.”

 

They lapsed into tense silence for a moment, Lillian watching Lena closely, intently, while Lena stared back with the look of a cornered animal waiting for the right moment to attack. Her mouth was dry and her palms clammy, glued to her chair with the distinct feeling of inadequacy and fear that had pervaded her childhood; Lena had never quite managed to get over it.

 

“What did he do to you?” Lillian eventually asked, her voice shockingly gentle and laced with sadness.

 

Looking away, a muscle twitched in Lena’s jaw and she closed her eyes, an assault of painful memories rising to the surface. Touching the middle of her forehead, Lena tried to settle them, fighting back the nauseous horror of what had happened. 

 

“I don’t want to talk about it.”

 

“Alright then.”

 

“You can go,” Lena dismissively replied.

 

“Not yet,” Lillian murmured, as if it was a suggestion and not an order. “I’d like to spend some time with you; it’s been enough years.”

 

Lips twitching with a slight sneer, Lena glanced at her from the corner of her eye. “You never bothered before.”

 

“I backed the wrong child.”

 

“I don’t care. I wouldn’t care if I never saw you again in my life. You made him; whatever was wrong inside him, it came from you .”

 

“You’re forgetting that I helped you. I arranged for you to meet him; you’d either be dead or still that limp imitation of yourself parading around idiotically if it wasn’t for me.”

 

Lena’s sneer was more obvious this time and she pinched the bridge of her nose as she squeezed her eyes shut. Moving quickly, uncrossing her legs and rising fluidly, danger in the bristling lines of her small frame, Lena stared at her mother with pure venom.

 

“I’m still that limp imitation , and I’m the thing he made me into as well. The only difference is that now I remember why I resent you so much. Go .”

 

“What’s going on?”

 

Lena’s head whipped around to the door, where Kara was standing, a bouquet of tulips in hand and a hard look of contempt on her face as she stared at Lillian. Rubbing at her forehead, Lena bit back a sigh and then let her hand fall back down heavily at her side before gesturing dismissively at her mother.

 

“She was just leaving.”

 

“On the contrary, we haven’t even gotten to the purpose of my visit,” Lillian drawled.

 

Stepping across the threshold, face stiff and the unmistakable air of her hidden power radiating from her, Kara gently closed the door and set the flowers down on the dresser before walking over to Lillian and grabbing her by the collar of her shirt as Lena rose to her feet, a warning on her lips. Yanking her close, Kara’s mouth tightened at the corners as she murmured quietly.

 

“She said you’re leaving.”

 

“Aren’t you the protective ex-guard dog,” Lillian mused. “Is the divorce all settled then?”

 

Jerking back as if bitten, Kara’s throat bobbed as her mask cracked and then slammed back into place. Her hand wrapped around Lillian’s throat and hauled her to her feet, eliciting a choked gasp of surprise at being so violently handled by her daughter-in-law. Setting her carefully on her feet, Kara fixed Lillian’s collar and stepped back jerking towards the door.

 

“Go.”

 

Casting Lena an appraising look, Lillian arched an eyebrow and smiled thinly. “So, I take it you’re not interested in taking L-Corp back?”

 

Lena’s stomach jolted, and her stiff expression hardened as she flushed slightly, looking down. “Keep it.”

 

She missed Lillian’s look of unabashed shock, knowing that the company was Lena’s pride and joy - or rather, had been when she’d been running it - and she sank back down onto the armchair, stooping to pick up her book. The pages were crumpled and she smoothed them out with shaking fingers, her stomach sinking with regret as she turned her back on one of the few things that had ever been hers. She’d made L-Corp into the force that it was, pioneered technology and been lauded for her achievements, and now she was reduced to a trembling, frightened shell of herself, struggling to make it through the day without breaking down. It was pitiful.

 

Kara’s hands were warm as they slid over Lena’s cold fingers, stilling the tremors in her hands as she knelt before her, looking up into her face with wide blue eyes. Her concern was palpable and Lena wanted to push her away. It seemed that was all she did these days, nursing her wounds and her pride in solitude. She couldn’t even begin to imagine facing Kal , the face of that little boy she’d shot burned behind her eyes, her son’s face morphing into the other one whenever she thought about him. 

 

“Hey, it’s alright. She’s gone now,” Kara murmured, giving her hands a gentle squeeze.

 

“I’m fine,” Lena hoarsely said, pulling her hands back and setting the book aside. 

 

Climbing to her feet, Kara moved over to the empty vase and deposited the fresh tulips in it, spreading the flowers out as the pop of colour brightened up the neutral room. She cleared her throat after a minute and turned to look at Lena, who had her face in her hands.

 

“I thought I might bring Kal tomorrow. It’s the weekend so he won’t have to miss school.”

 

Raising her head, her face gently devastated, Lena’s shoulders slumped. “I don’t think that’s a good idea.”

 

“It wasn’t him. It wasn’t you . You know that.”

 

Swallowing the sourness of bile at the back of her throat, Lena picked at her nails, the scabbed edges of her cuticles, the shakiness in her stomach, all of it making her feel sick. “It doesn’t matter. It was real, I remember it.”

 

“He misses you.”

 

“I miss him too.”

 

“It might help-”

 

“It won’t.”

 

Crossing over to the armchair across from hers, Kara sank down onto the cushion and braced her elbows on her knees, fingers laced in her lap. “You … are the strongest person I know. Every single bad thing that’s ever happened to you, you’ve just- you’ve locked it away, moved on as if it doesn’t affect you, and … that’s not fair. Lena, you can’t just pretend none of this happened, you don’t have to be strong and overcome it. Let me help you. Please.”

 

Softly clearing her throat as she tried to quell the knotted unease in her chest, Lena kept her eyes down on the cover of the book held in her hands, slowly turning it as she tried to distract herself, before she spoke, her voice low and shaking.

 

“Kara … you should go.”

 

“I won’t,” Kara murmured, her voice soft but defiant.

 

Mouth twisting as she let out a derisive scoff, Lena wiped at her eyes and looked towards the window, a muscle jumping in her jaw. “I don’t want you here, okay? I don’t need another person telling me how to- to feel and act. Nothing is going to make it all go away so just leave me alone. ”

 

“Lena-”

 

Shooting to her feet, Lena stalked away, her shoulders hunched and taut with tension, running a hand through her hair in an anxious manner. “I just want to forget. I wish- I wish I’d never remembered, I- if I’d been Tess, I could’ve been happier.”

 

Kara rose and gave her a strained smile, the words coming out thick and rasping as she faltered. “We both know you would never have been happy not knowing the truth.”

 

“Then you should have told me! Your fault. This is all your fault,” Lena snapped, her eyes bright with anger and her cheeks flushed with it as Kara shrank back, wounded. And then she blinked and her brow furrowed as she touched her fingertips to the spot between her eyebrows. “No. No, that’s not- no, it wasn’t you . It was him, wasn’t it? It’s- I’m so … confused. ”

 

The anger evaporated from her, replaced by a quiet confusion as she looked at Kara with lost green eyes. Blinking back tears, Kara slowly moved towards her, reaching out to cup her shoulders in her warm hands.

 

“It’s okay. Let me help you.”

 

“There are too many people inside my head,” Lena said, her voice shaking as she tried to hold it together. “I don’t know which one to believe; it all feels so real. It all feels like me.”

 

Tears traced down her cheeks and she let Kara pull her into a hug, her body going slack in her embrace as she sank into the person that felt at home in her arms. She’d known those arms for a decade, known the comfort, the strength and warmth, and it was enough to settle her, to straighten her out for a moment, before she drew in a deep, shuddering breath and exhaled sharply. Snapping back to herself with clarity, Lena pulled back.

 

She wiped her eyes on the heels of her palms and sniffed before letting out a short laugh. “I’m alright.”

 

“No, you’re not,” Kara miserably replied. “I thought- I hoped being here might- might help.”

 

“It does. Just not enough.”

 

“I- tell me what you want me to do,” Kara pleaded. “Tell me and I’ll do it.”

 

Shaking her head, Lena blew all the air out of her lungs and then laced her fingers behind her neck. Tipping her head back, she closed her eyes and was silent for a moment. “I want you to go to work and stop worrying about me.”

 

“I can’t.”

 

“Well, you can’t keep doing this.”

 

“I quit my job,” Kara blurted out.

 

Opening her eyes, Lena lowered her head and met her gaze. “What?”

 

“I quit. After I brought you here. I- there was a time when I prioritised being Supergirl over my family, over everything, when I should have put you first. And I’ve learned my lesson in the worst way possible so … I quit.”

 

“You can’t do that,” Lena protested, her face crumpling with frustration.

 

Kara let out a strained laugh, one side of her mouth hitching higher than the other. “It was actually very easy. Andrea knows that I’ve only been employed by name for the last four and a half years, so it wasn’t as if she was losing staff. You and I both know I haven’t been much of a reporter for a long time.”

 

“You love your job-”

 

“No, I love you,” Kara quickly blurted out before she went rigid.

 

Cheeks turning pink, Kara opened and closed her mouth as she cringed, letting out a strained laugh. “Sorry, I don’t- I mean … I care about you. I want to help you get better and … that’s more important than my job. I … fucked that up last time, and maybe we wouldn’t be in this mess if I hadn’t, so …”

 

“Don’t blame yourself.”

 

“Hard not too,” Kara said with a hollow laugh, wrinkling her nose.

 

Her composure cracked then as she smiled widely, eyes creasing at the corners and her blue eyes filling with tears. Drawing in a shallow breath to object, Lena was cut off as Kara swallowed and turned away, her eyes roaming the room.

 

“I, uh, I need to use the bathroom quickly.”

 

“Kara,” Lena inaudibly murmured, watching her walk over to the bathroom and shut herself inside.

 

She felt like crying, that aching pressure building in her chest as she covered her mouth with a hand. Standing in the middle of her room, swimming in regret, drowning in it, Lena listened to the sound of running water and Kara emerged a few minutes later, red-eyed and sniffing before she cleared her throat.

 

“Let’s go for a walk.”

 

They made their way outside, walking side by side along one of the paved paths, watching birds flit through the trees. The sky was a pale shade of blue and the wind blew in their faces as they walked past wilting flower beds, neither of them wanting to break the silence first. Lena knew Kara would be content for them to not speak a word, if that’s what Lena wanted. She’d visited enough times to face empty silence as Lena sank into her memories instead of rooting herself in the present. But Kara’s guilt was eating her alive and she could feel the weight of it as if she held it in her own cupped palms.

 

“It’s not your fault,” Lena whispered, the words coming out slightly breathless. She felt winded, faint. “It’s my fault. I left you. I left you. And then I was gone. I ruined your life. I took away any chance of you being happy. I’m sorry. I’m sorry, I- I know it’s been hell for you. I didn’t mean for this to happen. I didn’t mean to ruin your life.”

 

“You didn’t ruin my life,” Kara said with a choked laugh, a confused look clouding her face. “You were the first good thing to happen to me.”

 

Rubbing at her eyes, feeling restless and tired, Lena exhaled sharply. “I just- I don’t know what to do anymore. I- usually I can just … lock it away, put it all into boxes, but Doctor Park said … I can’t do that with this.”

 

Lips twitching with a ghost of a smile, Kara rubbed at the back of her neck. “I think you should listen to Doctor Park.”

 

“I have a natural mistrust of therapists.”

 

“I’m well aware,” Kara wryly replied, glancing sideways at her and burying her hands in her pockets. She hesitated, her expression turning grace for a moment as she looked ahead, brow furrowed. “You should know … I’ve started seeing someone.”

 

Shock flashed across Lena’s face and her stomach lurched, a breathless nausea sweeping through her as her vision narrowed. She felt as if she turned five shades paler, the word tipping around her as her chest constricted. “Oh, I, uh-“

 

“Kelly thought it might help me to … process all of this. I mean, I don’t have to tell you. You know I never really gave up and I think … I think that seeing a shrink, talking about it with someone, might- might help me too.”

 

Blinking as her mouth opened and closed, a vague sense of sheepishness swept through Lena and she made a choked sound at the back of her throat. Curling her clammy hands into fists, she swallowed dryly.  “Oh, um, you’re seeing … a shrink? That’s good.”

 

“Yeah, it is. I just- I want you to know that you’re not alone and I’m trying too. I just- I want you to get better. I want you to get better for yourself. And I want to help you do that, so I figured … I should deal with my own shit so I can … be in a position to- to support you when you’re ready to come home.”

 

Giving her a rueful smile, crooked and edged with pain, Lena nodded. “I’m trying.”

 

“I know you are,” Kara said, suddenly reaching out and grasping her hand for a fleeting moment, her touch strong and reassuring. “Take all the time you need. Just … think about seeing Kal, okay? He misses you.”

 

Looking down at the paving stones lining the path, Lena’s mouth thinned. “I miss him too.”

 

They spent a few more hours in the garden, Lena sitting cross-legged on the grass as she basked in the wan sunlight, letting her mind drift. She’d gotten marginally better at meditation after being subjected to it every day, and it was somewhat peaceful, even if she found it hard to stop her mind from drifting most of the time. Eventually, Kara had to leave when it was time for Lena’s second therapy session of the day, and she found herself filled with that reluctance to say goodbye as they parted ways with murmured promises to see each other tomorrow.

 

Sitting on the sofa in that comfortable room open to the gardens, Lena felt some of the lingering tension knotting her muscles as she tried to relax. Doctor Park eyed her closely and asked a few questions to ease into the session before the conversation became more direct.

 

“Kara visited again today. She hasn’t missed a visit yet.”

 

“She quit her job,” Lena explained.

 

“Oh. How do you feel about that?”

 

Mouth thinning, Lena shrugged half-heartedly. “She hasn’t really gone to work since I went missing. Her boss was- is my best friend so she didn’t fire her, but … I guess Kara should make her own decisions.”

 

“Could we discuss your relationship a bit more?”

 

Chewing on her lip, Lena shrugged again, forcing herself to sit back and cross her arms over her chest. Doctor Park leaned forward, curiosity in her warm brown eyes.  “You filed for divorce shortly before you went missing.”

 

Swallowing thickly, Lena curtly nodded. “Yes.”

 

“That’s a big decision to make. How did you know when it was over?”

 

Blowing the air out of her cheeks, Lena ran a hand over her face and then raked her fingers through her hair as she thought. It was hard to explain; she’d been in love with her, had never stopped, but each day felt much the same. Every day she was filled with that uneasy fear of what fresh injuries Kara would come home sporting - if she made time to come home before Lena went to bed. It had gotten to the point where so much had changed between them that Lena didn’t recognise the young woman standing before her as the young girl she’d fallen in love with. Along the way, she’d pulled away, resentment and misery eating away at her by her brother’s subtle manipulations.

 

“I think I just- I felt more in love with the memories we had together than the person standing in front of me. I still loved her, I just … I couldn’t go on.”

 

            “Loved?”

 

Opening her mouth, Lena inhaled sharply and then quickly closed her mouth again. She closed her eyes, letting Kara appear in her mind; the smell of her detergent, the warmth of her skin, the hardness of her muscles, the sound of her laugh, the way she’d used to whistle as she made waffles on the weekend - before she’d spent so much time away from them - how she’d cheered Kal on at soccer, only mere months ago, how she’d speak to him in Kryptonian and ruffle his hair, how she felt pressed up against Lena’s bare skin, kissing her. It made her chest ache, it made her miss her.

 

“Love,” Lena quietly admitted. “Of course I still love her. I just … outgrew her.”

 

Humming pensively, Doctor Park leaned back and crossed her legs. “You know, when someone tells me they outgrew someone, I always question them. Let’s break it down - you were growing and Kara wasn’t. That’s understandable. But did you try to help her grow? Did you try to work through it together?”

 

Lips pressed into a hard line, shame burned a hole through Lena and her reply was a long time coming, and unwillingly admitted. “No.”

 

“Why not?”

 

Ducking her head down, Lena grimaced, her chin dimpling as her eyes burned. “I … don’t know. I guess I just- I thought I knew how it would all play out. None of it changed anything.”

 

“Did it play out how you imagined?”

 

“No.”

 

“What changed?”

 

“I was kidnapped, and I would’ve given anything to- to go back and not be so damn proud and work things out.”

 

“And how do you feel now? After being home.”

 

Lena’s face screwed up and she rubbed at her eyes. “She’s like a completely different person. We both came back to each other so different. I don’t know how … I fell in love with her all over again. I don’t even know if that’s even true; maybe I just felt like I should’ve because I thought we were still married and wanted to make it easier to fill that hole. I don’t know.”

 

“Do you believe that?”

 

Hesitating, Lena slowly shook her head. “No. No, I- I really did fall in love with her again.”

 

“Have you communicated that with Kara?”

 

Swallowing, Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners. “Not … really. A little. It doesn’t matter now.”

 

“Why not?”

 

“Because I remember now. And I’m … trapped by the past.”

 

“Then open the door.”

 

Closing her eyes, Lena shook her head. “I can’t see the door.”

 

“It’s right in front of you, Lena. You’ll know when the right time is to reach out and open yourself up to the future. There’s no rush, and you’re the only person who knows when you’re ready for the next step.”

 

That step came a week later, lingering in a covered pavilion beside Kara as it rained around them, a cardigan over the sweatpants and T-shirt she was wearing as she leaned against the wooden railing. Kara was sitting on a bench, basking in the outdoors as she let her sensitive hearing tune into nature without the deafening sounds of the city. It had been a quiet hour, both of them reading together in companionable silence for the most part, and Lena eventually turned, bracing her elbows against the railing as Kara met her eyes.

 

“Can you bring Kal tomorrow?”

 

Surprise bloomed on Kara’s face and a small smile curled her lips as she deflated, quiet relief spreading through her. “Of course.”

 

Lena wasn’t entirely convinced she was ready but she missed him. He was her kid and she’d already missed out on so much, and it wasn’t so much a punishment for herself, but for Kal as well to keep pushing him away. Lena was just afraid that the guilt would consume her and she wouldn’t be able to look him in the eye, wouldn’t be able to hold him or let herself near him without feeling like a monster.

 

But she woke early the next day and had her morning therapy session with Doctor Park, nervously explaining the next step. It wasn’t quite opening the door, but it was a step towards it and Lena made an effort to get dressed into something that wasn’t sweatpants, even enduring a longer bath to wash her hair as her stomach tied itself into knots.

 

She didn’t know what time Kara would arrive - she’d said in the morning but not when - so Lena spent the grey morning in the gardens, sketching flowers as she tried to calm her nerves. Her palms were clammy and she kept fiddling with the pencil, the hours seeming to drag by until she heard a shout that jerked her head up.

 

“Aunt Lena!”

 

Her face went slack as she took in his dark, messy curls, his piercing blue eyes behind the glasses and his restraint as he ran towards her at a human’s pace. Kara followed behind, a small smile on her lips, and Lena pushed herself to her feet, latching onto the boy as she pushed aside the face of a different boy and held out her shaking hands. 

 

And she didn’t hurt him, didn’t feel quite so monstrous as Kal slammed into her with enough force to make her stumble back slightly. She didn’t hurt him as she wrapped her arms around him in a tight hug and squeezed her eyes shut, teeth grit so hard against the burning pressure of building tears as her throat closed up and her heart swelled with love, making her chest ache. He’d grown - just a little, but she noticed - and Lena had to choke back a sob, a wavering smile curled her lips as she held her son as herself for the first time in almost five years.

 

“Kal. I missed you.”

25. Chapter 25

            “Happy birthday.”

 

            Kara blinked, slowing mid-stride as she glanced down at the blueberry muffin Lena held aloft. There was a folded piece of paper and a plucked wildflower on top of it sitting on the bench, the breeze threatening to blow them away, and Kara looked surprised as she met Lena’s eyes.

 

            “You forgot?” Lena asked, her voice light with shock.

 

            Eyebrows rising and falling quickly as a series of expressions crossed her face, Kara let out a quick laugh, reaching for the muffin. “I did. Although, that explains why Alex invited herself over for Chinese food tonight.”

 

            Giving her a wry smile, Lena tilted her head to the side a fraction. “Sorry I can’t be there.”

 

            “Seeing as I forgot my own birthday, I won’t hold it against you,” Kara said with evident amusement as her face crumpled with bewilderment.

 

            She sank down onto the bench and Lena joined her, the day overcast and cool. They weren’t the only ones in the garden and Lena watched as a young pop star held a yoga pose on the lawn before she turned her attention to Kara. Fumbling for the folded piece of paper and the flower, Lena smiled thinly.

 

            “Best I could do was a muffin stolen from the dining hall and a shitty card made in arts and crafts, but …”

 

            Kara let out a choked laugh as she reached for the card, taking in the neat block letters coloured in red, blue and yellow as it spelled out Happy Birthday. Opening it up, Kara swallowed thickly, her eyes scanning the writing before she looked at Lena, giving her a watery smile, her eyes bright with unshed tears.

 

            “Your handwriting is the same again.”

 

            “Mm. Out of all of my personas, I definitely have the best one.”

 

            Wiping at her eyes as she tried to pretend that she wasn’t wiping away her tears, Kara cleared her throat but her words were still slightly hoarse. “There was a time when I didn’t think I’d ever get to see you again, let alone get a birthday card.”

 

            “I should’ve been there,” Lena murmured with bitterness.

 

            She had progressed to anger, feeling it over every slight injustice, every lost moment or regretful word exchanged. The weeks had passed by, September nearly over, and Kara brought Kal every Saturday and Sunday, staying all day as Lena played chess and checkers with him, played hide and seek in the gardens and finally went on a trail ride, Kal perched on a pony and Kara and Lena sandwiching him in ahead and behind. They made the most of their time together, trying to pretend like they weren’t at the clinic, like they were a family enjoying their day together. 

 

            Still, she was angry . Angry at herself for allowing herself to be so easily manipulated, angry at her brother for all the damage he’d done to her life, angry at Kara for lying and not fighting harder, for letting her walk away, angry at all of her friends for keeping her in the dark. She was even angry at Kal, for growing up so fast without her. It was with great reluctance and only encouragement from Doctor Park, that Lena had sought solace in the slow precision of martial arts sequences in the open gym facility, moving through different forms as she tapped into the part of herself that she hated most, hoping this time it would be the part of herself that offered an escape.

 

            When the trance-like repetition of moving through the sequences couldn’t calm her, she ran, miles and miles disappearing on the rubber track of a treadmill beneath the pounding of her feet, until she could barely stand and her joints protested at the rigorous pace. Sweating and flushed pink, Lena would sit in a cold bath and force herself to stay just that little bit longer. 

 

            There were all sorts of exposure therapy she was encouraged to try, someone never too far to ensure her safety. Lena still couldn’t stomach the thought of showering since regaining those horrific memories, the torture making her stomach twist, and once when she’d been caught out in the rain, she’d sank to her knees and curled in on herself, the water like acid as it pattered against her back. But she got used to the sluggish feeling of the medication, used to the touch of orderlies without fighting the instinct to slam them against the floor or wall, used to being around Kal as she tried to get past the memory of a different boy with a bullet in his head.

 

            “You know, it’s your birthday in a few weeks, then,” Kara mused. “We should do something. Maybe … you can finally let the others come and visit for a couple of hours. Have you thought about it much?”

 

            “A little. I- well … I’ll let them, but … only if you agree not to come those days.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            “It’s not that I don’t … appreciate it,” Lena haltingly continued, wincing slightly. “I just think … it’ll be good. For both of us. I think getting some space- and Kal … I know he’s never called us mom, but we’re the closest thing he’ll ever have, and I’m here, so it’s up to you now. Spend time with him - for me. Take him … to the beach, to the park, the zoo. Take him to Paris for the day. Don’t … sit here with me every day and waste all that time; all I ever wanted was for you to-”

 

            Trailing off, Lena’s mouth thinned as she swallowed, guilt creeping up on her. Kara gave her knee a quick pat, her head ducked down. “I know. I told you a while ago that … if you got your memories back, you’d be mad at how shit I’ve been as a parent.”

 

            “I’m mad at a lot of things, but not that,” Lena murmured. “I wish you hadn’t, but I understand why you did. Now’s your chance to make up for it, though.”

 

            “And what about your chance?”

 

            “Mine’s going to have to wait a while. He’s a kid, Kara, he doesn’t need to spend his every weekend with me. Take him to the movies. Send Alex to babysit me and go and do something fun .”

 

            Shoulders hunching as she twirled the stem of the flower between her fingers, Kara drew in a shuddering breath and then tipped her head back. Eyes squeezed shut, there was the slightest tremor in her chin as she exhaled through her nose.

 

            “I can’t,” she whispered, her voice cracking. “Every time I leave … I’m worried I’ll never see you again. I thought it got better, once I got you back, but it’s gotten worse since you got your memories back.”

 

            “I know. So am I,” Lena murmured. “But you have to confront that sooner or later.”

 

            “I wake up every day still thinking he’s alive, you know,” Kara admitted, letting out a shaky breath. “And then comes the relief that he’s- that I-“

 

            Lena reached out and raised Kara’s hand with the muffin in it, fixing her with a piercing stare. “If it’s any consolation, I finished it off. You didn’t kill him - I did. Now, eat your muffin.”

 

            Choking on a sob, Kara broke a piece off and popped it in her mouth and the two of them sat there sharing the remainder of it. They didn’t speak and Lena was weighed down with all the untold things within her, memories and feelings, some old and some new. Eventually, she worked up the courage to voice one of her thoughts.

 

            Turning to look at Kara, her brow furrowed slightly in apprehension and against the glare of the white sky, Lena bit her lip. “Doctor Park thinks it might be a good idea for you to join one of my therapy sessions soon.”

 

            Kara’s eyebrows rose a fraction and she turned to meet Lena’s stare. Uncertainty flashed across her face and she cleared her throat, crumpling the empty grease paper in her fist.

 

            “And what do you think?”

 

            Shrugging indifferently, Lena averted her gaze, frowning at the treetops as she picked at a splinter of wood on the bench. “I don’t know. It could be helpful.”

 

            “In what way?”

 

            Exhaling softly, she closed her eyes. “I know you’ve seen the tapes but … I have a hard time talking about any of it. I’m working on that. It’s … painful, and I hate it, but she thinks talking about what happened before might help as well.”

 

            “The divorce?”

 

            “Yeah. That.”

 

            “Oh. Okay. If that’s what you want.”

 

            They waited until the following week to have that session, Kara showing up in the morning, wary as she rubbed her hands on the thighs of her jeans and crept into the room looking guilty. Lena was sitting at one end of the sofa and Kara sat at the other as she quietly greeted them both.

 

            It felt awkward, almost unbearably so as Lena glanced sideways at her, Doctor Park watching them both closely for any reaction. She smiled kindly at Kara as she laced her fingers together and leaned forward slightly.

 

            “Thank you for being here today, and thank you, Lena, for opening yourself up to trying a new approach.”

 

            Nodding in acknowledgement as she propped her cheek in her hand, Lena’s eyes darted between the two women. She didn’t speak and felt even more nervous and uncooperative as she tried to swallow the shaky feeling rising within her.

 

            “Now, I always like to try and get couples in for a session when possible, just to try and clear the air. Make sure everyone’s on the same page with any unvoiced issues that may be holding us back from our personal journey. Our growth. Lena, perhaps you’d like to go first?”

 

            Resenting it just a little, guilt eating away at her as she tried to stifle the memory of crying in a cell by herself, regretting so many things but regretting leaving more than anything else. How could she voice that? Kara had seen the tapes, knew she would’ve changed things if she could, but it had been too late for that and too many years and so much pain had slipped by.

 

            “Where should I start?” she asked, her tone curt.

 

            With a placating smile, Doctor Park tilted her head to the side. “How about you start with one thing you’ve been holding back from saying to Kara?”

 

            “I’m not holding anything back,” she quickly lied. Closing her eyes as she exhaled softly, Lena pressed her mouth into a thin line. “I mean … you saw the tapes my brother left behind; you know what happened so … that’s all I want to share. For now.”

 

            Opening her eyes, Lena stared at Kara’s curious face, guilt knifing through her. Doctor Park hummed quietly and then turned her attention to Kara.

 

            “Kara? Perhaps you’d like to say something you've been holding back?”

 

            Shifting, Kara opened and closed her mouth, staring at the coffee table as she struggled for a moment. “I- there is, but I … I don’t know how to ask it.”

 

            “Honesty and directness is most effective in therapy.”

 

            Lena felt stiff and coiled with anticipation of Kara’s words and she waited for what felt like forever for her to eventually speak. When she did, meeting Lena’s eyes, her expression was sad and confused.

 

            “You said before that you didn’t fight because … you already knew how it would play out, but … why. Why didn’t you give me a chance?”

 

            Lips twitching with a rueful smile as her eyes shone brightly, Lena swallowed thickly. “Because I felt like my life was just … falling apart, and I was losing myself in the process. I felt so lonely. And if I’d known he was behind it, maybe I would’ve made more of an effort to get past it, but … it wouldn’t have changed anything.”

 

            “Yes, it would’ve,” Kara firmly insisted, her voice tight and raw. “It would’ve changed everything. I would’ve been there, I wouldn’t have let him take you. We could’ve been happy instead of … whatever we are now.”

 

            “No, you couldn’t have. The only difference would have been you being caught instead of me.”

 

            “I would’ve preferred that.”

 

            Doctor Park raised a hand before Lena could respond and leaned forward. “Why would you have preferred that, Kara?”

 

            Taking a moment to construct her answer, Kara looked up at the ceiling as she chewed on the inside of her cheek. “I would rather endure anything, anything in the universe, before I let it hurt her. It wouldn’t have mattered if we were- if we weren't together; I would’ve asked him to take me instead. I could’ve lived with that, but I couldn’t live without her. My life has been hell. For four years, I’ve just … existed. I haven’t had any life, I haven’t been happy. And I just- I think if she’d asked me to fight, it might’ve been me instead of her, and I would’ve been a hell of a lot happier for it.”

 

            Lena scoffed, “you would’ve been happy to go through what I did?”

 

            “If it meant you didn’t have to, yes, I would’ve.”

 

            “That’s easy to say.”

 

            “It’s true.”

 

            Clenching her teeth, Lena exhaled sharply through her nose and rubbed her eyes. “You might be able to physically fight your way through things, but some things are psychological. You wouldn’t have survived it; you weren’t raised to compartmentalise like that.”

 

            “I didn’t say I would’ve survived it, only that I would’ve done it to spare you,” Kara quietly replied, her voice firm as she curled her hands in her lap.

 

            “Okay, there seems to be some underlying tension here,” Doctor Park warily interjected, “how about we try and unpack that?”

 

            Kara let out a strained laugh at her suggestion and gave her a thin smile. “The underlying issue is that I am- was Supergirl. That’s the catalyst of this entire situation. The root of my guilt, the cause of our divorce, the centre of all of our problems and Lena’s anger.”

 

            “Oh, I, uh … okay. Lena, do you- do you want to talk about that anger?”

 

            Raking a hand through her hair, Lena’s eyes were bright with annoyance as she shifted on the seat. She had the urge to punch something and closed her eyes as she breathed slowly, trying to centre herself with the meditation tools she’d been working on.

 

            “I am angry. I’m angry at a lot of things. I’m angry that I- that I felt like I had no other choice. I didn’t marry Supergirl.”

 

            “But you did.”

 

            Opening her eyes, she gave Kara a mournful look as her face crumpled. “I didn’t. I married you - I never cared about what you could do, I never cared about those other people. Yes, that’s selfish of me, I know, but I would’ve picked you over the entire world - I did , multiple times while helping you - and I just- I got sick and tired of taking a backseat in my own marriage. I got tired of some car accident being more important than our anniversary. It was killing me; I felt like I was slowly dying every day that you prioritised other people over your own family. Saving them was selfless, yes, but it was selfish too. You were selfless with yourself but selfish with your time for your family.”

 

            “Lex-“

 

            “I know it was him,” Lena angrily replied, fingers hastily wiping away tears. “I know it was him now, but we didn’t at the time. At the time it just- it felt like I was losing the only thing that had ever been mine. And then you became everyone else’s but mine. I was so fucking lonely and you just- you weren’t around.”

 

            “I could’ve been,” Kara said, a plea in her voice. “If I’d known-“

 

            “I shouldn’t have had to tell you,” Lena sharply retorted. “I shouldn’t have had to beg for you to just stop. Honestly, I thought I was doing us both a kindness by just putting us out of our misery. I thought we both would’ve been happier if we could do what we wanted.”

 

            Blinking back tears in her wounded eyes, Kara swallowed thickly. “Were you?”

 

            Deflating as she let out a forceful breath, Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners. “No, of course I wasn’t. I knew if I held out long enough I would get used to it though. And we’d be better off like that.”

 

            “You shouldn’t have made that decision for me,” Kara said, her voice raw and cracking as she wiped her eyes on the cuff of her sleeve.

 

            “No, I shouldn’t have had to.”

 

            “You-“

 

            Doctor Park cleared her throat, “how about we re-centre?”

 

            Lena squeezed her eyes shut and hesitated, a tightness in her chest as she drew in a shaky breath. “Actually, uh, can we- can we stop here? I have a headache.”

 

            Before waiting for a response, Lena climbed to her feet and stalked out of her room. She was irritable and restless, walking back to her room and pacing back and forth as she tried to muddle through the confusion of her old and new feelings, revolving around the manipulation, how every fault between them had been so perfectly orchestrated to slip knives into every single one of Lena’s vulnerabilities. He’d known her so well, known exactly what her limits would be and she felt sick and angry and devastated.

 

            Forty minutes later, the door opened and she stopped her pacing to find herself facing Kara. Paling slightly, she took in the dark spots of rain dotting Kara’s shirt, her blonde hair darkened where it stuck to her face in damp strands.

 

            “I thought you left,” Lena quietly broke the silence.

 

            “I wouldn’t have - not without saying goodbye first. I just- I had to clear my head. Went for a walk in the gardens.”

 

            Nodding, Lena twisted her hands before her and kept her eyes downcast as Kara slipped inside, easing the door shut. She sighed softly but was silent for a long minute before taking a step forward.

 

            “I know so much of what I did was wrong,” Kara said. “I know I let you down. I should’ve put you first - you and Kal - and I should’ve appreciated you more. I get why you did it, and … I’m not mad. I mean … I was, but I had a long time to stew in it and realise there were worse things than divorce. I just want you to be happy now, that’s all.”

 

            Mouth twisting ruefully, Lena closed her eyes. “After all this time, I still feel like shit when we argue.”

 

            “Yeah,” Kara hoarsely replied. “I’d still take it over missing you any day.”

 

            “I know I haven’t been fair to you-“

 

            “No, I think it’s been pretty fair,” Kara said with a short laugh.

 

            Lena’s lips twitched with a ghost of amusement as she shook her head. “No. I’ve been a bit uncompromising. I know how hard it’s been for me; I also know it’s been hard for you, I just don’t know how. I’m trying not to blame you for too much. I’m taking responsibility for my part too.”

 

            “Don’t.”

 

            “We both hurt each other. We just- we never got to resolve any of it before it all went to shit. But … I think I had it easy because I didn’t have to live with the memories of it all for a while.”

 

            Kara choked on a laugh. “Oh, yeah. Must’ve been a walk in the park for you, right?”

 

            Lena snorted, rolling her eyes as they stung with tears. Walking over to an armchair, she sank down onto it and drew her legs up to her chest. She propped her chin on top of her knees and brooded as Kara slowly crossed over and took a seat across from her.

 

            “Kara,” she started before faltering, her voice wavering as she closed her eyes. 

 

            Taking a deep breath, she tried again, speaking around the lump in her throat and the heaviness in her chest. “Kara, I want you to be happy too. I hope you know that. I- it wasn’t fair of me to choose for you but … I don’t want you to give it up. Put the suit back on; do what makes you happy.”

 

            “Happy?” Kara choked, thumbing away a tear. “Lena … it never made me happy to do it. I did it because I felt like I had to. It all started because I was trying to save someone I loved; I never wanted to do it for any other reason than that. I was eighteen . I was a kid; I just wanted to go to college. All it ever brought me was- was stress and so much anxiety that it felt like I couldn’t breathe, trying to save everyone at once. You were the only thing that gave me a pause … until you were the reason I stopped completely.”

 

            She ran a hand over her face and let out a broken laugh as Lena stared at her, pale and wary and nursing her broken heart.

 

            “I know you think that I neglected you,” Kara whispered, her voice halting and breaking as she spoke, a certain impatience to get it off her chest as she picked at the cuff of her shirt. “The truth is … I spent every hour of the day crushed by the weight of who I am. Every hour I was awake, I worried about someone I loved dying, about some disaster demolishing the city, of some invasion or enemy I couldn’t stop. And when I slept, I dreamt of all the ones I’d already fought before but I lost to them instead. And then I’d wake up, and it would start all over again. I would wake up and the thought of losing you would just immediately paralyse me. The only way I could manage it was by overcompensating, by beating everything he set against me and every tiny crime.”

 

            “You never told me any of that.”

 

            “I didn’t want to worry you. I didn’t- I didn’t want to burden you with it, and the price of keeping it from you turned out to be higher than I thought. I just … I made a mistake.”

 

            “You did what you thought was right. Same as I did.”

 

            “It doesn’t feel that way. All I know is … I’m done.”

 

            Lena’s cheeks dimpled as she grimaced and she forced herself to swallow, a faint headache forming behind her eyes as she tried to parse through her conflicted emotions. A few years ago, she would’ve given anything for Kara to stop, for them to fix things, but now it just left a bitter taste in her mouth as guilt crept over her.

 

            “I don’t want you to give it up for me.”

 

            “It’s not for you - I’m choosing to do it. I don’t want to spend the rest of my life prioristing people who don’t matter over people who do. It wasn’t Supergirl who saved you. It wasn’t Supergirl saving the city while I was searching for you for four years; it was J’onn, and Alex, and Kelly, and Nia and Brainy. If they can manage it, then … I’m superflous to the task.”

 

            “And what if they can’t manage it? There might something that’s so strong that it makes their powers obsolete. It’s happened before.”

 

            Gesturing vaguely, Kara’s face spasmed with pained amusement. “Then I’ll step in, if I have to.”

 

            “We both know you can’t sit by and let innocent people die,” Lena stated before her expression clouded and she cocked her head to the side. “But … you did . I- sorry, it’s just- it gets a bit confusing sometimes. There’s such a big gap in the middle that sometimes … it feels like you just changed overnight in my mind.”

 

            “I did change overnight. I’m sorry I’m not the same person you fell in love with, but … I have more spine now. I guess I’m not as … uptight.”

 

            Lena let out a spluttering laugh, “well, I wouldn’t have described you that way.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose, Kara grinned sheepishly and shook with quiet laughter. “I was though, wasn’t I? Always so morally upstanding . Always so optimistic. I feel like I was the cause of so much of my own unhappiness.”

 

            “You were the first good thing I ever had,” Lena murmured. “I loved that about you. So much. With everything with my family, optimism and upstanding morals were … refreshing. I just- I felt like sometimes you pretended more than you let on. I would’ve rathered love the version of you that admitted she was scared than the one who pushed everyone away while saving the world.”

 

            Nodding, Kara pressed her lips into a flat line and bowed her head for a moment before speaking. “Can I ask you something?”

 

            “As long as I can choose to answer,” Lena warily replied.

 

            Smiling thinly, Kara narrowed her eyes in a piercing, searching look. “When did you choose to leave? What was the final straw? That moment where you just … knew.”

 

            Tipping her head back, Lena inhaled deeply and then blew all the air out of her lungs. She blinked a few times as she looked up at a thin crack in the ceiling and picked at the arm of the chair, trying to collect her thoughts. She knew the moment, of course she did, but she felt old pain tear through her, that frustration and anger and resignation. It had been awful and it was just another old wound she didn’t want to poke at.

 

            “Um, it was- I was working late. You picked Kal up from kindergarten and … there was some sort of emergency. You left him by himself. I got an alert from Hope and I went home as fast as I could - I got two speeding fines. I’d barely gotten inside and found him pulverising his Lego blocks in the bedroom before you were back. You didn’t think I would find out, but you just- you left him unsupervised. Just for fifteen minutes. You insisted he was fine, that because he was smart and starting to come into his powers he had the maturity to be left alone. I shouted at you and you stormed off and then … the next morning I called my lawyers and asked them to write up the papers.”

 

            Letting out a strained laugh, Lena dabbed at her eyes and sniffed, her brow crumpling in a troubled look. Kara closed her eyes, a ragged look of anguish tightening her expression as she rocked slightly on her seat.

 

            “I remember that,” she whispered. “Car accident just before the harbour bridge. Head-on collision between a semi-truck and a minivan. The minivan spun out and went off the road; it was balancing on the edge of the cliff by the time I got there. It was going to go over any second - the dad was unconscious, blood everywhere, the mom was screaming her head off. They had four kids in the back. The oldest was seven; her head was bleeding and she was trying not to cry. The youngest was only a few months old; he was still in a carrier. I lifted the car out, called an ambulance for the dad. The mom had two broken legs. You should’ve seen the state of the car.”

 

            “You didn’t tell me that.”

 

            Mouth hitching into an uneven smile, edged with wry bitterness, Kara rubbed at the back of her neck. “You didn’t want to know.”

 

            Averting her gaze, a prickle of shame knifing through her, Lena let out a shaky breath. “I know I was stubborn-”

 

            “It’s still no excuse,” Kara quickly cut her off. “I just- I think because my parents used to do things like that with me … I thought it was okay to do it too. But they sent a kid off to raise a baby so … well, they weren’t very responsible. Weren’t very good people either. I never wanted to be like them.”

 

            “You weren’t - aren’t .”

 

            “I just imagined such a different life for myself. Then I got sent here and I lost it all. And then I found you , and I thought it would be okay, and then we had Kal. We grew up so fast and … I don’t think I was ready for any of that. There are so many things I regret; we shouldn’t have rushed to get married, you shouldn’t have put off college to be a mom, I should never have put on the suit.”

 

            “None of that would’ve changed anything.”

 

            “Wouldn’t it? Tell me, when you left, how did you feel? Once you knew you got away from it all. Did you feel happier?”

 

            Falling silent, Lena didn’t respond for a long minute, the tension between them so thick that she thought she might cry over how unbearable it all felt. “No. Of course I didn’t feel happier . I was heartbroken. It was devastating to leave you. But … I felt relieved . Underneath all the awful guilt and pain, I just- I was relieved that it was over, one way or another.”

 

            Cracking her knuckles, Kara smiled wanly, “I know how that feels. That’s how I felt when I found you again. Just relieved you were back, regardless of whether you were my Lena or not.”

 

            “I don’t think I’ll ever be that person again.”

 

            “Maybe not. I think we’ve both changed too much since then. We can only hope it wasn’t all for the worse.”

 

            Her smile was a shade more genuine then, her blue eyes holding a dim twinkle, and they lingered in silence for a while before she eventually had to go. Chest aching, Lena watched her climb from her seat and made a few promises about giving her more breathing room, about sending Kelly tomorrow instead and taking Kal to the Appalachians for some flying, before Kara made for the door.

 

            “Hey, Kara?”

 

            Pausing at the soft sound of Lena calling after her, Kara raised her eyebrows expectedly, her hand on the door handle as she lingered.

 

            “Thanks for staying. I feel better- well, not better but lighter , having finally talked about it.”

 

            Giving her a crooked smile, Kara’s eyes creased at the corners behind her glasses. “It was a bit overdue.”

26. Chapter 26

            True to her word, Kara sent Alex and Kelly the following day and took Kal to the movies. The thought of not seeing her for a day was unusual after so long without a break but the first glimpse of Alex and Kelly being escorted through to the gardens, where Lena was enjoying filling out a crossword book Kara had brought her on one of her visits, made her realise just how much she’d missed her friends. For so long, they’d been a part of Lena’s family, and it stung a little to think that there had been a rift between them all in her amnesiac state. 

 

            It was bittersweet to finally realise everything she’d been missing out on, and Lena tucked her pencil in between the pages and set the book down as she climbed to her feet. Feeling a little self-conscious and reserved in her pyjamas and cardigan, Lena offered them a wavering smile as the distance between them shrank.

 

            “Hey,” Lena murmured, the sound drawn out and full of yearning as the feeling of missing her friends hit home for the first time.

 

            She might have seen them occasionally after coming back, but it was no sort of friendship. Spending all of her time around Kara had made her feel less confused about the gap there, but there was a giant gap where Alex and Kelly had been and she felt a little overwhelmed to be meeting them again under normal - or as normal as could be expected - circumstances.

 

            Kelly got to her first, hesitating before she engulfed Lena in a tight hug, both of them quietly laughing as they rocked slightly. Lena felt the stinging of tears build behind her eyes and Kelly pulled back, smiling widely.

 

            “It’s good to have you back.”

 

            Nodding, Lena blinked rapidly and turned her attention to Alex, who hugged her as well, chin on her shoulder and hands splayed across her back, her voice a little rasping when she spoke. “Thank God. I mean, we knew- she said, but … God , we’ve missed you.”

 

            “Yeah,” Lena replied, her voice cracking as she pulled back and sniffed, “I’ve missed you both too. I … sorry, this just all feels a bit surreal.”

 

            Kelly nodded with understanding, reaching out to rub her back as she looked at her with concern. “How’re you doing?”

 

            “I-”

 

            Faltering, Lena opened and closed her mouth and eventually worked out a choked sound, shaking her head. Reaching up to wipe her nose on her sleeve and dab at her eyes with the cuff of her cardigan, she swallowed thickly. Her cheeks warmed and she felt mildly embarrassed at how quickly her composure unravelled.

 

            “It’s okay,” Kelly murmured.

 

            “I just- it’s … hard,” Lena eventually ground out, closing her eyes and turning her wet cheeks skywards. “It’s getting better, but then stuff like this happens and I realise … just how much has changed. And I wish I could just … go back. I miss how it all used to be.”

 

            Alex let out a quick laugh and gave her a dubious look, trying to break the pall of grief that had descended over Lena. “How it used to be? Are you sure?”

 

            A breathless laugh got caught in Lena’s throat and her face crumpled with confused amusement before she let out another laugh. The heaviness in her chest alleviated slightly and she sniffed, wiping at her cheeks.

 

            “Well … I could do without the failed marriage. Hey, congratulations, by the way. I know we celebrated over that God-awful  dinner but now remember you enough to actually be thrilled about it,” Lena said with a wry smile, gesturing to the engagement ring on Kelly’s left hand. “Set a date yet?”

 

            “Not yet. We’ll probably wait until everyone’s … in a better place. Bigger things to focus on, you know?” Alex said with a small smile, her brown eyes flitting over Lena’s face. 

 

            Smiling crookedly, Lena looked down at her hands. She’d always loved Alex, always ached to have a sister like her, someone to have her back and help her through the tough things, and her chest ached for a second as she thought about how she’d had Lena’s back without her even knowing. For once, someone had picked her, been loyal to her , and she was struck by a sudden feeling of gratitude to her sister-in-law. Things had been a little uncomfortable during the split, but she was glad she’d never lost them in the process.

 

            “You know, I thought you were just being a little bit of an ass before because I wasn’t myself,” Lena said with a hoarse laugh, a wavering grin crossing her face as she met Alex’s eyes, “but now I realise you were just trying to protect me, so … thank you for having my back. I know it wouldn’t have been easy being mad at her.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Alex slung an arm around Lena’s shoulders in such a casual manner that Lena didn’t have time to stiffen at the abrupt contact. “Yeah, well, Kara’s an ass sometimes. I wish she would’ve told you; it would’ve saved you both some heartache. Maybe I should’ve told you myself, but-”

 

            “She’s your sister. I know.”

 

            “She was wrong for that.”

 

            Humming in agreement, Lena closed her eyes and stifled the aching in her chest. “We were both wrong about a lot of things.”

 

            “Let’s sit,” Kelly murmured, gesturing to Lena’s favoured bench.

 

            Sinking down onto the bench, placing her crossword book in her lap, Lena was quiet and reserved for most of their visit, smiling softly and content to listen to them regale her with stories and venture a few safe questions. Kelly knew better than anyone how to handle her fragile state, her work with PTSD leaving her more in-tune to Lena’s occasional bouts of odd silence as she struggled to stay present, and she was quick to ease her through it with some ridiculous memory to drag her back out of it. They didn’t comment on the moments when she wrapped her arms around herself and tap her shoulders, eyes closed as she breathed slowly, evenly, grounding herself again in between their laughter and joking.

 

            They came again the next weekend, and then Kelly on a day where she only had clients scheduled in the morning. Slowly but surely, there was a rotation of her friends visiting; J’onn joined her in the garden for meditation when the weather was nice or played chess in one of the communal spaces when it was raining. Brainy came with Nia, the latter bringing good coffee and gossip while the former brought science and engineering magazines and talked tech with her, which felt natural and gratefully distracting. 

 

            But still, Lena enjoyed the days with Kara and Kal the most, playing soccer or card games, making paintings in the art room and talking about school and the newest cartoon he’d watched. On the day's Kara didn’t visit, Lena missed her sorely, but she never told her. She envisioned Kara at home, doing laundry, feeding Odysseus and ordering takeout while she read books and watched TV. She imagined her getting brunch with Nia on the days Alex was visiting, and dinner with Alex and Kelly on the days they didn’t visit, walking in the park and browsing boutiques. Maybe she took Kal for ice cream at that parlour after soccer games and to the museum, staring at the same paintings she’d gone to see a dozen times before. Lena was incapable of thinking of much else except for her - when she wasn’t consumed by her own mind.

 

            The weeks slipped by and things felt a little more settled. Therapy got easier, the rapport between her and Doctor Park well-established by that point, and the doses of her medication had been tinkered with until she didn’t feel nauseous and sluggish, in fact, felt better than she had in a while. The orderlies encouraged her to sit outside in the pale sunlight for at least an hour a day, breathing in the fresh air, and it got to the point where Lena’s mind didn’t stray as easily in meditation. She exercised every day, moving through the motions and stances of the didn’t forms she’d been programmed with, and sometimes ached for something to punch to unleash the anger that was balled up inside her.

 

            When Kara visited, it no longer felt awkward or uncomfortable, like they were skirting around taboo topics - although they very much were - but they lied to themselves for the sake of peaceful days spent walking the short trail through the woods, sometimes on horseback, of watercolour paintings in the arts and crafts room where Lena had finally started sketching the old nightmares for all their horrifying truth. They were analysed in her private therapy sessions, and in the group ones, she would venture the occasional comment when asked, although she never bridged the gap between herself and the others. Sitting in a circle, she would watch the other patients and itch to escape, to go home.

 

            Lena turned twenty-seven on an unremarkable day towards the end of October, the weather grey and cold and her whole family there to celebrate. They brought a cake and balloons and a stack of gifts, and she opened them with Kal, exclaiming over each item in the private room they’d secluded themselves in for the impromptu party. Afterwards, they listened to music and ate cake and took turns playing velcro tennis on the lawn outside until it started raining and everyone trickled off until it was just Kara and Kal left.

 

            They played checkers and Pictionary in one of Lena’s sketchpads until the sun started to set, and Lena hugged Kara just a little bit longer and a little bit tighter when they left before dinner. It was the first birthday in almost five years she hadn’t spent alone, and she went to bed that night with a lightness in her chest that had evaded her for so long. It was healing to have them all there, to fit in that empty spot again, as if she’d never left. 

 

            November quickly arrived and the month was almost halfway over when Doctor Park held one of their morning sessions, just after meditation, and spent the first half of their session observing her closely with a satisfied look on her face. Her words caught Lena by surprise when she spoke, revealing the words she’d held back since the beginning of their session. 

 

            “I think you’re ready to go home,” Doctor Park said, a small smile on her face as her eyes shone with pride.

 

            A jolt of panic flashed through Lena and she straightened up, shoulders stiffening as she felt like she’d gone three shades whites. Mouth dry, she opened and closed her mouth as a tightness constricted her chest.

 

            “No, I’m not,” she quickly objected.

 

            “Why do you think that?”

 

            “I … there’s still so much- I’m not … better. I- I can’t go home until I’m better.”

 

            “Lena,” Doctor Park gently spoke, leaning forward, “you know that isn’t the purpose of therapy. It’s to help you understand , to come to terms with the parts of yourself that are affecting your ability to integrate well with society. We’ve made some real progress here - you might not see it because you’re holding yourself to a higher standard, to who you were before, but it’s true. That progress continues after you go home as well, this just means you’re well enough to grow and heal and adjust away from here. You should be proud of yourself.”

 

            Shaking her head, Lena stared back at her with wide, panicked eyes. “No, I- it’s- I can’t. I need to be fixed first-”

 

            “Fixed is an interesting term. Do you think that you’re broken?”

 

            “Yes,” Lena whispered, her mouth twisting with hatred for having to admit that. “Yes, of course .”

 

            “In what way?”

 

            Drawing in a shuddering breath, Lena closed her eyes, wrapping her arms around herself and squeezing tightly. “I’m not the person I used to be. I can’t- I can’t take showers . I can’t … I can’t go back to that house, or my apartment. I can’t forget everything up here.”

 

            Touching her fingertips to her brow, Lena hung her forehead and exhaled sharply. She felt unbalanced by the mere thought of going home, but the truth was that none of the things she’d stated was the things that were stopping her. It was true that she couldn’t stand the thought of water lashing against her without being violently dragged into horrid memories of Arctic waters and electroshock, or that the thought of going back to the apartment she’d been dragged from and the house she’d departed covered in blood with her brother’s dead body in the foyer, but the one overwhelming thing that stopped her from going home was Kara.

 

            There would be nothing delaying the conversations they needed to have, and Lena was terrified of the thought of having to finally open the floodgates to everything she’d kept tucked away while in the Fortress of Solitude. And more since then, so much to wade through to even meet each other halfway that the thought of having to confront it made her reluctant to leave. It was cowardly of her, but ideally, she would be able to stay here a while longer and they could linger in the strange bubble they existed in, putting off the inevitable indefinitely. 

 

            “Lena,” Doctor Park replied, stretching out the sound of her name as she raised her eyebrows slightly. “You know this only works if we’re honest with each other.”

 

            Licking her lips, Lena’s eyes darted around the comfortable room. The room she’d spent two hours in every day for more than three months now. The thought of leaving this place and never sitting on that sofa again made panic prickle across her skin, a lump formed in her throat, but Lena knew that she was no longer a danger to herself or others. She’d managed to sort through the horrors inflicted upon her and integrate the three versions of herself 

 

            “I’m not ready to … confront everything outside of here.”

 

            “Ah. Well, that’s the good thing - you’re in control of your own life. You’re allowed to take your time and figure things out when you’re ready. All this means is that you’re allowed to continue growing outside of these walls, but that doesn’t mean that the work is done yet. It’ll become a less intense approach - three sessions a week via video call with me, a monthly check-in with Doctor Hamilton. Over time, we’ll reduce our time together to once a week, but only once you’re at that point.”

 

            “Why can’t I just do that here?”

 

            Deliberating for a moment, Doctor Park hummed. “You could , but that would only delay the inevitable. You’ve done the hard part, Lena. You’re a resilient person, you- you’ve done really well. It may not seem like it to you, but what you endured … it’s something that another person might not have been able to survive. You’re a survivor. All you can give yourself now is time. Time and space to feel it all, to process things at your own pace. You have a good support network outside; I’m confident that you’ll be able to assimilate well.”

 

            Apprehension made Lena stiff as she stared at the psychologist who had borne witness to numerous breakdowns, from the very lowest point of her recovery to the strides she’d made in putting in the work. She trusted her, trusted her methods and her patience, the kind demeanour that made it feel like no matter what she said, it was never inconsequential or dismissed. Lena knew she was just hiding behind this treatment here, had felt complacent for a couple of weeks now, going through the motions of the same day, finding comfort in routine familiarity.

 

            Still, she wasn’t sure whether giving up that routine was worth the consequences of facing her wife, feeling the unbearable tension between them that made Lena’s skin feel like she was on fire, remembering every single intimate moment between them, every fight, every bit of tenderness. Just being near Kara in a monitored setting was enough for Lena to feel like she might explode, and she was hesitant to remove that buffer, knowing it was the only thing stopping the floodgates from opening.

 

            “What if I don’t?” she asked, her voice small and gravelly, the rims of her eyes a little pink as she fought back helpless tears.

 

            “Recovery isn’t a straight road. Maybe it’ll loop back around here again, maybe it’ll fork off to a different practitioner to continue therapy with. Maybe once you’re out of here, you’ll hit a boulder in the road and it’ll take a while to figure out how to get around it. All of that’s okay ; we all take our own journey at a different pace. There’s no right way to heal. There’s no right way to handle trauma.”

 

            Nodding as her chin wobbled, Lena closed her eyes and swallowed thickly. “I just … I have to open the door.”

 

            “Exactly,” Doctor Park softly exclaimed. “It’s time to open the door, if you’re ready.”

 

            It was another week of talking about it, keeping the idea from Kara on her visits, before Lena felt like perhaps that was the right step to make. She couldn’t hide away there forever - she had a family, a business, a life to get back to - but the idea was enough to twist her stomach into knots. It was even harder to find the courage to voice the frightening prospect as well, but on a clear November morning, sitting on the lawn as she huddled in a sweater and sipped a cup of steaming tea, waiting for the rain to arrive, the conversation arrived on its own.

 

            “Have you started Christmas shopping yet? What about his birthday party?”

 

            “Mm. You’re missing out on all the fun,” Kara said with a crooked grin.

 

            Smiling thinly, Lena shrugged nonchalantly as pain blossomed in her eyes. “It’ll be the first in five years for me; it would be fun.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose, Kara grabbed her knees and rocked back slightly, baring her teeth in a grimace. “Sorry, that was a bit insensitive.”

 

            Laughing, Lena’s expression crumpled. “No, it’s fine. I just … sometimes I think about everything I missed out on. I mean, he’s going to be nine in a couple of weeks, and I know I was gone for half of it but when did that happen?”

 

            “I worry about the day he’s grown up enough to think he can start using his powers,” Kara murmured, her expression clouding. “Right now, he’s written a letter to Santa asking for a lightsaber and Transformers and the new Pokémon game and … I just think about how soon all of this will be over, and he’ll grow up and think he knows better than us.”

 

            “Shit. I forgot that kids believe in Santa. Does he still think the tooth fairy is real?”

 

            Kara’s answering laugh was loud and she unwound herself from her ball, stretching out her legs and leaning on her elbows.

 

            “No. He doesn’t even believe in Santa either. He just wrote a letter because that’s what they were doing in school.”

 

            “Oh, thank God. I was going to say, our kid is way too intelligent to think that a man in a flying sleigh brings him gifts. His cousin’s a literal superhero.”

 

            “He found out when he was six and stayed up all night listening for Santa to arrive, and instead he heard me cursing the house down while I tried to put his bike together in the kitchen. I still get milk and cookies out of it though.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Lena scoffed. “Is he still going for the dinosaur-themed party?”

 

            “Yeah. I picked the cake you suggested and the museum is closing for it, thanks to our very generous donation to their palaeontology department.”

 

            Plucking a withering leaf from the grass, Lena twirled the stem between her fingers and smiled tenderly. “He’ll love it.”

 

            “Yeah,” Kara said with a satisfied sigh before her eyes strayed to Lena and she gave her a rueful smile. “I just- I wish you’d be there for it too.”

 

            Blinking in surprise, Lena tossed the leaf and rubbed her clammy palms on the knees of her sweatpants and shifted restlessly for a moment. Clearing her throat, she swallowed and stared at the damp blades of grass, bent where they’d trampled them.

 

            “Actually … they want to send me home soon,” Lena murmured, looking down at her hands.

 

            Kara was still beside her for a moment, watching her closely before responding. “Oh. That’s good.”

 

            Shrugging slightly, Lena’s mouth thinned with a ghost of a smile as she raised her head but didn’t meet Kara’s eyes. “I guess so.”

 

            “You’re nervous,” Kara observed, her eyebrows rising slightly. The Lena she knew wasn’t nervous about anything.

 

            Lena shrugged again, her mouth twitching at the corners as she slumped on the ground. “A little,” she admitted, hardening her stare as she narrowed her eyes at the daytime TV host speaking with her publicist. “It’ll just be … a strange adjustment, I think.”

 

            “You don’t want to go back home.”

 

            Resenting Kara’s ability to see through her veiled words, remembering just how perceptive her wife could be when she paid attention, so tuned in to the minute changes to Lena’s expression after knowing each other for so long. It seemed strange that Kara had found her so unreadable for the eight months she’d been back as someone else, so different to the Lena she’d been that even her guarded expressions were inscrutable.

 

            Letting out a short sigh, Lena ran a hand through her hair. “It’s not so much that. I just- I think it’ll be hard to be there again. After everything.”

 

            “Then why don’t we go to Midvale for a while?” Kara suggested.

 

            Meeting her gaze, Lena blinked and the tension seemed to bleed out of her. Midvale. The place they’d met, the place they’d fallen in love and gotten married and spent weekends and holidays as a family. It was all so detached from the painful things that Lena felt immediate relief sweep through her. 

 

            But that was also the place where things had gotten complicated again, where residual tension from a forgotten marriage that her body remembered had boiled over into something more , the two of them using each other to fill some void. She almost felt as if Kara could sense her thoughts, read it on her face what she was thinking of, remembering as she balled her hands into fists in her lap. 

 

            “Sure,” Lena eventually said, the word strangled as she looked away. “It’ll be good to see Eliza; she must have missed you a lot.”

 

            “Yeah. Just another thing to make amends for.”

 

            Reaching out, Lena closed her hand over Kara’s, a furrow forming between her brows. “Don’t be so hard on yourself. It’s my fault you-”

 

            “It’s not your fault,” Kara quickly cut her off. “Don’t say that.”

 

            “I won’t if you don’t.”

 

            Kara laughed at the coy smoothness in Lena’s voice, leaning back on the grass, legs stretched out before her and the white sky bleaching the gold out of her. She looked well-rested though, healthy and relaxed without the pinched look of grief and guilt that had plagued her since late January when she’d brought Lena back home. She almost looked like the Kara that she’d been before, just a little harder around the edges and not quite as restless, as if the weight of the last few years had settled something inside her.

 

            Reaching out, Kara offered her a hand and squinted as she smiled. “Deal.”

 

            Preparations were made for Lena to leave after that. Kara had meetings with her and her case managers, all of them sitting around a table as they drank coffee and discussed Lena’s care plan for once she was back home. It was evident she’d be with Kara, that they were caught in the middle of it all, the status of their relationship put on pause while Lena worked through everything. There was an understanding between Lena and Doctor Park that this was the cause of Lena’s reservations about leaving, that she was worried that this bubble they’d existed in would pop once they were thrust back into normal life, outside of the safety the clinic provided.

 

            Still, the day before Kal turned nine, Lena had her last therapy session at the clinic and helped a nurse back the belongings she’d accumulated over the last three months. It felt like an eternity had passed within the walls of the lodge, with its pale furniture and soothing artwork, everything seemingly muted and turned down. To someone who’d lost whole years , it was a huge chunk of time to be squirrelled away in the foothills of National City, but it was safe. Lena couldn’t remember the last time she’d been given a break, the time to do nothing and have nothing expected of her, without a threat to her life. She was almost sad to see it end and nervous to see what came next.

 

            Kara was shaking the hands of all the nurses and doctors, Lena’s duffel bag slung over one shoulder and the sleeves of her shirt rolled up to expose forearms corded with muscle, while Lena followed behind her, wearing real clothes for the first time in a while as she quietly thanked the people who had cared for her for weeks. It was Doctor Park who walked outside with them, reminding Lena of their session in two days’ time, and Lena was struck with the odd sensation that she would miss their daily sessions, that she owed this woman, who she knew virtually nothing about, so much .

 

            As Lena said goodbye, Kara stowed her bags in the trunk and lingered until she was climbing into the car, settling against the cool leather and balling her hands in her lap as her stomach swooped. Climbing in beside her, Kara slammed her door shut and buckled her seatbelt before pausing for a moment, looking over at Lena.

 

            “Are you ready?”

 

            Nodding, Lena swallowed thickly, shifting in her seat before nodding again. “Yes,” she finally rasped and Kara gave her a small smile before starting the car.

 

            They didn’t go home to their house though; Kal’s birthday party was tomorrow and they would be leaving for Midvale after that, which left them spending the night at Alex and Kelly’s house. It was cold when they pulled up outside the house, the front door opening as Lena climbed out and Kara went to fetch her bags, Alex standing in the doorway with Kal as she smiled softly at Lena, who hesitated. Eyes flickering over the front of the house, she felt as if she was seeing it with new eyes; although she’d been there since returning, they’d been living in an apartment when she’d vanished, and it felt refreshingly unfamiliar.

 

            “Hey,” Lena murmured, a weary smile softening her face as she opened her arms and wrapped Kal in a tight hug, kissing the top of his dark head as she basked in the feeling of being a mom again.

 

            “You must be tired,” Alex commented, jerking her head inside. “Why don’t you get settled in? Kelly’s making coffee.”

 

            They all shuffled inside, Kara bringing up the rear, and Alex directed them upstairs, Lena following Kara’s instructions to the bedroom she’d been put in. The double bed seemed far too large for her to sleep in alone after months in the narrow hospital-style bed but the room was homely and she sank down onto the mattress with a heavy sigh.

 

            “You alright?” Kara asked, setting the bag down at the foot of the bed.

 

            “Yeah, I’m … fine.”

 

            “It must be strange for you.”

 

            Shrugging, Lena gave her a crooked smile. “My life’s been strange for the past eleven months. I think this is one of the more normal things to happen, actually.”
